domain.title: Mathematics
domain.tag: linear algebra · calculus · probability · information theory · optimization
domain.why: This is the part everyone wants to skip, and you can't. The good news: the actual list of math you need for the rest of this path is much smaller than a full math degree — you don't need most of what a university math major studies. The bad news: the part that IS on the list is genuinely load-bearing. You can't fake your way through a neural network with vibes about what a gradient is; you need to actually be able to compute one.

people.name: Gilbert Strang
people.contribution: MIT 18.06 and Introduction to Linear Algebra. The 'four fundamental subspaces' framing used throughout this domain is his, and 18.06's problem sets are the ones we tell people to actually finish.
people.note: No social accounts listed on his MIT page; the OCW course pages are the canonical link.

people.name: Grant Sanderson
people.contribution: Essence of Linear Algebra and Essence of Calculus: the visual intuition for determinant-as-volume, change of basis, and the derivative as a linear approximation that the L3 layers here lean on.
people.note: Handle confirmed from the links on 3blue1brown.com; also on Bluesky at bsky.app/profile/3blue1brown.com.

people.name: Sheldon Axler
people.role: Professor Emeritus of Mathematics, San Francisco State University
people.contribution: Linear Algebra Done Right, which builds the spectral theorem without determinants. Our reservation: it is the wrong first book for an engineer who needs matrix computation as a working tool — read it second, after 18.06.
people.note: No social accounts on his site.

people.name: Lloyd N. Trefethen
people.role: Professor of Applied Mathematics in Residence, Harvard University
people.contribution: Numerical Linear Algebra (with David Bau), which is where the QR-over-normal-equations discipline in this domain comes from, plus Spectral Methods in MATLAB and the Chebfun project.
people.note: Moved from Oxford to Harvard in 2023; no social accounts listed.

people.name: Nicholas J. Higham
people.contribution: Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms — the standard reference for the conditioning-versus-stability distinction, backward error analysis, and matrix functions. Also the 'What Is...' series on his blog.
people.note: Died 20 January 2024; the account and blog are dormant but remain up. Handle taken from the Twitter card metadata on nhigham.com.

people.name: Cleve Moler
people.contribution: Wrote the original MATLAB as a front end to LINPACK and EISPACK, which is why 'the matrix is the unit of computation' is the default mental model. Numerical Computing with MATLAB is free.
people.note: Cleve's Corner is archived and no longer updated; no handle listed there.

people.name: Terence Tao
people.contribution: Analysis I/II, the standard route into the epsilon-delta material this domain treats selectively, and the expository blog posts on concentration, random matrices and measure that sit behind several L3 layers here.
people.note: Primarily on Mastodon now: https://mathstodon.xyz/@tao, linked from his own blog. No X account listed.

people.name: Judea Pearl
people.contribution: Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems and the do-calculus. The reason 'explaining away' appears in the conditional-independence concept, and the reason correlation-versus-causation is a structural claim here rather than a slogan.
people.note: No handle listed on his UCLA page; could not verify one first-party.

people.name: Andrew Gelman
people.role: Professor of Statistics and Political Science, Columbia University
people.contribution: Bayesian Data Analysis (BDA3, free PDF) and Stan. The 'garden of forking paths' paper is why the multiple-comparisons and p-value concepts here are framed as researcher-degrees-of-freedom problems.
people.note: Writes daily on his blog rather than social media; no handle listed on either Columbia page.

people.name: David J. C. MacKay
people.role: Physicist and information theorist, University of Cambridge (1967-2016)
people.contribution: Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms — free, and the only text that wires entropy, Bayesian inference and neural networks together in one argument. The compression-as-prediction concept here is his framing.
people.note: Died 14 April 2016. The book remains freely available at inference.org.uk; there is no living account to link.

people.name: Thomas M. Cover
people.contribution: Elements of Information Theory with Joy A. Thomas: the source for the AEP, typical sets, the data-processing inequality and channel capacity as they are stated in this domain's information-theory section.
people.note: Died 26 March 2012; his co-author Joy A. Thomas died in 2020. Historical entry, no account.

people.name: Stephen Boyd
people.role: Professor of Electrical Engineering, Stanford University
people.contribution: Convex Optimization with Lieven Vandenberghe, free from Cambridge, plus CVX and CVXPY and the EE364A lectures. The first five chapters are the high-value core referenced by the preserved Text concept.
people.note: No social accounts on his Stanford pages.

people.name: Sebastien Bubeck
people.role: Researcher at OpenAI; previously VP of Applied Research, Microsoft Research

people.name: Marc Peter Deisenroth
people.role: DeepMind Chair of Machine Learning and AI, UCL

sections.t: How to actually learn this as an adult engineer

L0.body: The unit of study is not the hour, it is the worked problem. Daily budget: 90 min minimum, of which >= 60 min is pen moving on paper. Log it: date | topic | problems attempted | problems finished unaided.
L0.cloze: Ninety minutes {{c1::a day, every day}} beats {{c2::ten hours on Sunday}}; every problem worked {{c3::by hand on paper}}.

concepts.L1: Ninety minutes a day, every day, beats ten hours on Sunday by a wide margin. Every problem worked by hand on paper. Reading mathematics passively produces the feeling of understanding with none of the substance, and the gap is invisible from the inside until you try to use it.
concepts.L2: This is the single highest-value item in the entire document, and it is the one people skip.
concepts.L3: Two mechanisms. Consolidation: memory traces are strengthened during sleep, so N sessions separated by N sleeps produce more durable encoding than one session of N times the length — the marginal value of hour six on Sunday is close to zero. Retrieval: generating a solution creates a memory that reading a solution does not, because the retrieval path itself is what gets strengthened. Passive reading exercises recognition, and recognition is the fluent, comfortable, useless cousin of recall. The paper matters because it removes the option of skipping the step you cannot do; on screen you scroll past it.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {hours} free hours this week for mathematics and a full-time job the following week. Schedule A: {hours} hours on Sunday. Schedule B: {hours}/7 hours each day. Which produces more retained skill four weeks later, and by what mechanism?
L4.answer: Schedule B, by a wide margin. Mechanisms: overnight consolidation between sessions, spaced retrieval, and the collapse of marginal attention late in a long session.
L4.explanation: Equal total hours, unequal spacing. The spaced schedule gets N sleep-mediated consolidation events and N retrieval opportunities against the massed schedule's one, and avoids the fatigue tail where a Sunday session stops producing encoding at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: You read a proof of {theorem}, followed every line, felt it was clear, and closed the book. Name the specific failure this creates and the single cheapest test that exposes it.
L4.answer: It builds recognition, not recall or generative ability. Cheapest test: close the book and reproduce the proof on blank paper.
L4.explanation: Fluency while reading is driven by the text supplying every next step. Blank-page reproduction removes that scaffold and the gap appears in seconds.

L0.body: Card front: 'Define: rank of A'. Card back: '$\dim (\mathrm{col}(A))$; equivalently the number of linearly independent columns, equivalently of independent rows'. Statements and definitions only — never a card whose back is a multi-step computation.
L0.cloze: Anki, {{c1::five minutes}} daily, for {{c2::definitions and theorem statements}} only.

concepts.L1: Anki, five minutes daily, for definitions and theorem statements only. Mathematics has a large vocabulary component that engineers systematically underestimate.
concepts.L2: A forgotten definition silently invalidates every argument built on it. You won't notice; you'll just find the next chapter incomprehensible and blame the author.
concepts.L3: Forgetting is roughly exponential in time since last retrieval, and each successful retrieval flattens the curve. Scheduling reviews just before predicted failure — what SM-2 and FSRS approximate — maximises strengthening per minute spent. The restriction to definitions is deliberate: definitions are atomic, unambiguous, and have a single correct answer, which is exactly the payload SRS handles well. Procedures are not; a card asking you to invert a 3x3 matrix has a long answer, high grading noise, and is better trained by solving problems.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these belongs on an Anki card? (a) 'State the definition of {term}'. (b) 'Compute the {op} of this 3x3 matrix'. (c) 'State the {thm}'. Justify the exclusion.
L4.answer: (a) and (c)
L4.explanation: (b) is a multi-step procedure: long answer, noisy self-grading, and it is trained by working problems, not by flashing. SRS is for atomic recall items.

L4.prompt_tpl: You cannot follow a proof that repeatedly uses the phrase '{phrase}'. Before blaming the author, what is the first thing to check?
L4.answer: Whether you can state the definition of that term cold, without looking.
L4.explanation: The usual cause of an incomprehensible chapter is a decayed definition three chapters back, not authorial obscurity.

L0.body: precalc -> single-variable calculus -> linear algebra -> multivariable calculus -> probability -> optimization -> information theory. Gate on each: can you solve unseen problems from the previous stage unaided, at speed?
L0.cloze: Precalculus repair -> {{c1::single-variable calculus}} -> {{c2::linear algebra}} -> multivariable calculus -> {{c3::probability}} -> optimization -> information theory.

concepts.L1: Precalculus repair → single-variable calculus → linear algebra → multivariable calculus → probability → optimization → information theory. Roughly 3-4 years at 90 min/day from a genuinely weak base.
concepts.L2: Attempting linear algebra before you're fluent with functions and algebraic manipulation is the most common failure. The blocker is almost never the new concept; it's the assumed fluency.
concepts.L3: Each stage consumes the previous one as free background. Linear algebra proofs manipulate sums and functions without comment; multivariable calculus assumes single-variable derivatives are automatic; optimization assumes both plus linear algebra; information theory assumes probability. When a prerequisite is merely known rather than automatic, it occupies working memory that the new material needs, and the new material then feels impossibly hard for reasons that have nothing to do with the new material. The 3-4 year figure is at 90 min/day; at 12 hours a day the wall-clock compresses but the ordering does not, because consolidation is time-bound, not effort-bound.

L4.prompt_tpl: A learner is stuck on {topic} in linear algebra. They report that the definitions are clear but every worked example loses them halfway. Give the two most likely root causes, in order of probability.
L4.answer: 1) Non-automatic algebraic manipulation (fractions, summation notation, factoring) consuming working memory. 2) A decayed definition from earlier in the same course. Genuine conceptual difficulty with the new topic is third.
L4.explanation: 'Definitions clear, examples lose me' is the signature of a fluency deficit rather than a comprehension deficit — the examples are where assumed background gets exercised.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given the recommended sequence, which of these comes strictly before {later}?
L4.answer: Everything earlier in: precalculus, single-variable calculus, linear algebra, multivariable calculus, probability, optimization, information theory.
L4.explanation: The list is a total order; each stage is assumed background for the next. Attempting optimization before multivariable calculus is the usual failure: the gradient and the Hessian are prerequisites, not notation.

concepts.t: Expect six to twelve months of feeling stupid

L0.body: Track a leading indicator that is not 'do I feel smart': problems solved unaided per week, and time-to-first-idea on a new problem. Both improve months before the feeling does.
L0.cloze: Six to twelve months of feeling stupid is {{c1::the process working}}, not {{c2::a signal to stop}}.

concepts.L1: This is the process working, not a signal to stop. Every adult who has done this reports it. The people who quit, quit here.
concepts.L2: Related: your engineering seniority actively hurts here. You are used to being competent, and returning to genuine beginner status is psychologically harder at 35 than at 18.
concepts.L3: The felt sense of difficulty is a poor proxy for learning rate, and in this regime it is anti-correlated with it: desirable difficulty — effortful retrieval, errors, slow generation — produces more durable learning than fluent processing, while feeling considerably worse. Add an expertise-reversal effect: a senior engineer's identity is built on rapid competence, so the same objective struggle carries a much larger identity cost than it does for an eighteen-year-old who expects to be bad at things. The fix is instrumentation, not willpower — measure unaided problems per week and let the number, not the mood, decide whether to continue.

L4.prompt_tpl: After {months} months you still feel lost daily, but your unaided-problem count has gone from {a} to {b} per week. Continue or change approach?
L4.answer: Continue. The objective indicator is improving; the feeling is expected and is not evidence.
L4.explanation: Feeling lost is the standard experience of this phase. The decision variable must be an objective one — unaided problems solved — because the subjective one is known to be miscalibrated here.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does this phase hit a {years}-year veteran engineer harder than a first-year undergraduate?
L4.answer: Identity. The veteran's self-model is 'competent quickly'; genuine beginner status contradicts it, adding an identity threat on top of the ordinary difficulty. The undergraduate has no such model to defend.
L4.explanation: Same objective struggle, very different cost. Naming it as an identity effect rather than an ability signal is what keeps people in the chair.

L0.body: The exact list: fraction and exponent laws, factoring, completing the square, log/exp identities $(\log (ab)=\log a + \log b, e^{\ln x}=x)$, function composition and inverses, summation notation, basic trig identities, inequalities. Test: simplify log(x^3 y) - 3 log x in one line.

concepts.L1: Not 'all of high school maths' — a specific short list: exponent and log laws, factoring, completing the square, function composition and inverses, summation notation, inequalities. Each must be automatic, not merely recallable.
concepts.L2: The list is short enough to finish in weeks, which is why skipping it is so expensive: people spend a year fighting linear algebra because sigma notation still costs them conscious effort. Completing the square in particular reappears verbatim in Gaussian densities and in quadratic optimization.
concepts.L3: Working memory holds roughly four chunks. A linear algebra proof already spends three on the objects it manipulates; if expanding $\sum_{i} (x_{i} - m)^{2}$ costs a chunk, the proof no longer fits and comprehension fails for reasons that look like conceptual difficulty. Automaticity means the manipulation runs without conscious attention, freeing the slot. This is why the repair pass is about speed, not correctness: being able to do it slowly is not the same competence. Diagnostic: set twenty mixed manipulation problems and require them at roughly thirty seconds each.

L4.prompt_tpl: Simplify to a single logarithm: log(x^{a} y) - {a} $\log (x)$.
L4.answer: $\log (y)$
L4.explanation: $\log (x^{a} y) = a \log x + \log y$, so subtracting a log x leaves log y. If this took more than a few seconds, the repair pass is not finished.

L4.prompt_tpl: Complete the square: $x^{{2}}$ + {b}x + {c}.
L4.explanation: For $b=6, c=5: (x+3)^{2} - 4$. This exact move produces the Gaussian exponent's mean and variance and turns a quadratic objective into an obviously-minimised form.

L4.answer: Split the sum over the addition, pull the constant c out of the first sum by distributivity, and note the second sum adds d to itself n times.
L4.explanation: Linearity of summation. It appears in every derivation involving means, variances and losses; it must be invisible.

prereqs: numeracy:Powers, roots, and the index laws
numeracy:Exponent laws with negative and fractional indices
numeracy:Function notation: f(x) is not multiplication
numeracy:Composing functions, and undoing them: inverses
numeracy:Sigma notation: a sum written as a loop

L0.body: Protocol: read the proof until each line is clear. Close the book. Reproduce it on blank paper. Diff against the original. Re-attempt only the steps you missed. Repeat at 1 day, 1 week, 1 month.
L0.cloze: Read the proof, {{c1::close the book}}, reproduce it on {{c2::blank paper}}, then {{c3::diff}} against the original.

concepts.L1: Read a proof, close the book, reproduce it from nothing, then diff. The diff is the entire value: it names the steps you cannot generate, which are invisible while the text is in front of you.
concepts.L2: Most people re-read instead, because re-reading feels productive and blank-page recall feels like failure. Re-reading measurably does not work for generative skill. Also: reproduce the proof's structure, not its wording — if you can state the strategy in one sentence before writing a line, you have it.
concepts.L3: This is the testing effect applied to derivations. Retrieval practice produces larger long-term gains than restudy at equal time, and the gap widens with delay. The diff step converts a vague sense of shakiness into a specific list of missing inferences, which is what makes the next pass cheap: you re-study three lines rather than three pages. The structural framing matters because proofs are compressible — rank-nullity is 'pick a basis for the null space, extend it to a basis for the whole space, show the images of the extension are a basis for the column space'. Store the sentence; the algebra regenerates from it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compress the proof of {thm} to a single sentence of strategy, then say which line of the full proof you would most likely fail to regenerate.

thm: the spectral theorem for 2x2 symmetric matrices

L4.answer: For rank-nullity: 'basis of the null space, extend to a basis of the domain, show the images of the extension vectors form a basis of the column space'. The commonly-failed line is the independence half of that last claim.
L4.explanation: Strategy sentence first, algebra second. The step you cannot regenerate is the one to drill, and it is almost never the first step.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {mins} minutes with a proof you half-understand. Spend them re-reading it {n} times, or reading once and attempting one blank-page reproduction?
L4.answer: Read once, then attempt the blank-page reproduction.
L4.explanation: Restudy raises fluency and confidence without raising retention much; one retrieval attempt beats several restudies at equal time, and additionally produces a diff you can act on.

L0.body:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[4., 7.], [2., 6.]])
assert np.allclose(np.linalg.inv(A) @ A, np.eye(2))
assert np.isclose(np.linalg.det(A), 10.0)
L0.cloze: np.{{c1::allclose}}(A @ np.linalg.inv(A), np.{{c2::eye}}(2))  # never use == on floats

concepts.L1: Do the derivation by hand, then check it numerically on a small random instance. Ten lines of numpy turns 'I think the gradient is 2Ax' into a fact, and turns a silent misunderstanding into a failing assert.
concepts.L2: This is a check on your maths, not a replacement for it — running the code first destroys the exercise. And the check must be random: identity-shaped or symmetric test cases hide exactly the errors you are most likely to make, such as a transpose in the wrong place, which only shows up on a non-symmetric matrix.
concepts.L3: A hand derivation and a numerical evaluation are near-independent error channels, so agreement is strong evidence and disagreement localises the bug fast: bisect the derivation, checking each intermediate quantity against numpy until the first mismatch. Randomised small instances are the key design choice — a 3x4 non-symmetric matrix with distinct entries breaks the symmetries that mask transpose errors, index swaps and layout-convention mistakes. Use np.allclose, never ==, because floating point equality is not the relation you mean; and use a fixed seed so a failure is reproducible.

L4.prompt_tpl: You derive $\nabla_{{ x }} (x^{{ T }} A x) = 2Ax$ and test it on A = np.eye({n}). The test passes. What class of error does this test fail to detect?
L4.answer: Anything involving A's asymmetry — the correct general result is $(A + A^{T})x$, which coincides with 2Ax only when A is symmetric. The identity is symmetric, so it cannot distinguish them.
L4.explanation: A symmetric or identity test case is invariant under transposition, so it is blind to transpose errors. Test on a random non-symmetric A; there 2Ax and $(A+A^{T})x$ differ.

L4.prompt_tpl: With A = [[{a}, {b}], [{c}, {d}]] and $x = [1, 2]$, compute both 2Ax and $(A + A^{{ T }})x$ and report whether they agree.

L0.cloze: In $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, addition and scalar multiplication act {{c1::componentwise}}; a vector is an arrow from the origin OR a {{c2::list of coordinates}} in a chosen basis.

concepts.L1: A vector in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is simultaneously an arrow with direction and length, a point, and a list of n numbers. Addition is tip-to-tail; scalar multiplication stretches and, for negative scalars, flips. The list of numbers is coordinates relative to a basis you have silently chosen.
concepts.L2: The coordinates are not the vector. [3, -1] means 3 of one basis vector plus -1 of another; change the basis and the same arrow gets different numbers. Holding this from day one is what makes change of basis and 'the gradient is basis-dependent' land later instead of arriving as a shock.
concepts.L3: $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is defined as the set of ordered n-tuples with componentwise operations, and every arrow-picture claim reduces to that definition. Tip-to-tail addition is the parallelogram law, which holds componentwise because $(v+w)_{i} = v_{i} + w_{i}$ in each coordinate independently. Scalar multiplication $c\cdot v$ scales length by $|c|$ since $\|c v\| = \sqrt{\sum c^{2} v_{i}^{2}} = |c| \|v\|$, and reverses direction when $c < 0$. The 'silently chosen basis' is the standard basis $e_{1}\dots e_{n}$: writing $v = [v_{1},\dots,v_{n}]$ is exactly the statement $v = \sum_{i} v_{i} e_{i}$.

L4.explanation: $2u = [6,-2,4]; 3v = [-6,12,3]$; difference = [12,-14,1]. Verified in numpy. Scalar multiples distribute over the difference componentwise, which is the entire content of the vector-space axioms at this size.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compute the Euclidean length of u = [{a}, {b}, {c}].
L4.explanation: $\|u\|^{2} = 9 + 1 + 4 = 14$, so $\|u\| = \sqrt{14} \approx 3.74166$. Verified in numpy. Length depends on the basis only through the inner product; in the standard basis it is the square root of the sum of squares.

L4.prompt_tpl: The same physical arrow has coordinates [1, 1] in one basis and [2, 0] in another. Explain how both can be correct.
L4.answer: Coordinates are the coefficients needed to build the arrow from a specific basis. Different bases need different coefficients for the same arrow.
L4.explanation: If $b_{1} = [1,1]/\dots i$.e. the second basis contains a vector pointing along the arrow at half its length, the arrow is 2 of it and 0 of the other. The arrow is basis-free; the numbers are not.

L0.body:
$\mathrm{span}\{v_{1}, \dots, v_{k}\}$ = { c1 v1 + ... + ck vk : ci in R }.
Is b in span{v1,v2}?  Solve $[v_{1} v_{2}] c = b$.
np.linalg.solve(np.column_stack([v1, v2]), b)
L0.cloze: A linear combination is {{c1::$c_{1} v_{1} + \dots + c_{k} v_{k}$}}; the span is the set of {{c2::all}} such combinations, and it is always a {{c3::subspace}} through the origin.

concepts.L1: A linear combination is a weighted sum of vectors. Their span is the set of every vector reachable that way — a point, a line, a plane, or all of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. Asking 'is b in $\mathrm{span}\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\}$?' is exactly asking whether the system $[v_{1} \dots v_{k}]c = b$ has a solution.
concepts.L2: Span is about reachability, not about the specific vectors: {[1,0],[0,1]} and {[1,1],[1,-1]} have identical spans. And span always contains the origin (take all $c_{i} = 0$), which is why a line not through the origin is not a span, and why affine layers need a bias term to escape that restriction.
concepts.L3: Closure gives the subspace property: if $x = \sum c_{i} v_{i}$ and $y = \sum d_{i} v_{i}$ then ax + by = sum (a ci + b di) vi, again a linear combination, so the span is closed under addition and scaling. Dimension of the span is at most k and is exactly k when the vi are independent. The reachability question reduces to solvability: b in $\mathrm{span}\{v_{1}\dots v_{k}\}$ iff b is in the column space of the matrix with those columns, iff Gaussian elimination on $[V | b]$ produces no row of the form [$0 \dots 0 |$ nonzero]. That single reduction is why every 'can I express this?' question in the subject becomes a linear system.

L4.prompt_tpl: Is b = [{b1}, {b2}] in span{{[1,2], [3,-1]}}? If so give the coefficients.
L4.answer: Yes: $b = 2\cdot [1,2] + 3\cdot [3,-1]$; coefficients (2, 3).

L4.prompt_tpl: What geometric object is span{{[1,2,3], [{a},{b},{c}]}} in $\mathbb{{ R }}^{{3}}$?
L4.answer: A line through the origin.
L4.explanation: $[2,4,6] = 2\cdot [1,2,3]$, so the second vector adds no new direction. The span of two parallel vectors is one-dimensional.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why the set of points on the line y = {m}x + {c} (with c nonzero) is not the span of any set of vectors.
L4.answer: Every span contains the zero vector, obtained by taking all coefficients zero. A line with nonzero intercept misses the origin, so it cannot be a span.
L4.explanation: This is exactly why an affine layer is $Wx + b$ rather than Wx: the bias translates the image off the origin, which no linear map can do.

L0.body:
$v_{1}\dots v_{k}$ are independent iff  $c_{1} v_{1} + \dots + c_{k} v_{k} = 0 \Rightarrow c_{1} = \dots = c_{k} = 0$.
Equivalently: $\mathrm{null}(V) = \{0\}$ for $V = [v_{1} \dots v_{k}]$, equivalently $\mathrm{rank}(V) = k$.
np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.column_stack([v1,v2,v3]))
L0.cloze: Independent means the only solution of {{c1::$c_{1} v_{1} + \dots + c_{k} v_{k} = 0$}} is {{c2::all $c_{i} = 0$}}; equivalently no vector is a {{c3::linear combination of the others}}.

concepts.L1: A set is linearly independent when the only way to combine it to zero is with all-zero coefficients. Equivalently: no vector in the set is redundant — none lies in the span of the others. Dependence means at least one direction is being counted twice.
concepts.L2: The definition is stated with 'equals zero' rather than 'no vector is a combination of the others' because the zero-form is what you can actually compute with: it is a homogeneous system, and Gaussian elimination answers it in one pass for any k. The intuitive form requires k separate checks.
concepts.L3: Suppose $\sum c_{i} v_{i} = 0$ with some cj nonzero. Divide by $c_{j}: v_{j} = -(1/c_{j}) \sum_{i \neq j} c_{i} v_{i}$, so vj is in the span of the rest and is redundant. Conversely if vj is such a combination, moving it to the other side gives a nontrivial relation. So the two formulations coincide. Computationally, independence of the columns of V is the statement $\mathrm{null}(V) = \{0\}$, which elimination decides: independent iff every column is a pivot column iff $\mathrm{rank}(V) = k$. Corollary used constantly: any $k > n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are dependent, since rank <= n < k.

L4.prompt_tpl: Are the columns of [[1,2,3],[2,5,7],[3,7,{d}]] independent? Answer for d = {d}.
L4.answer: $d=11$: determinant 1, independent (rank 3). $d=10$: determinant 0, dependent (rank 2).
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: $\det = 1$ for $d=11$ (rank 3, independent); $\det = 0$ for $d=10$ (rank 2, dependent — column 3 = column 1 + column 2).

L4.prompt_tpl: Can {k} vectors in R^{n} be linearly independent?
L4.answer: No.
L4.explanation: Rank is at most $\min (k, n) = n < k$, so the k columns cannot all be pivot columns; a nontrivial null vector exists. More than n vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are always dependent.

L4.prompt_tpl: Prove that if a set contains the zero vector it is dependent.
L4.answer: Take coefficient 1 on the zero vector and 0 on all others: the combination is 0 with a nonzero coefficient, so the relation is nontrivial.
L4.explanation: A one-line proof that is worth being able to produce instantly; it is the smallest case of 'a redundant direction'.

L0.body:
A subspace S: closed under + and scalar *, contains 0.
Basis of S: independent set that spans S. $\dim (S)$ = number of vectors in any basis.
Coordinates: $x = \sum_{i} c_{i} b_{i}$; solve $B c = x$ for c.
L0.cloze: A basis is {{c1::independent}} and {{c2::spanning}}; every vector then has {{c3::exactly one}} representation in it, and dim is the size of any basis.

concepts.L1: A subspace is a set closed under addition and scaling that contains the origin. A basis is an independent spanning set: independence removes redundancy, spanning guarantees coverage. Its size is the dimension, and every basis of a given subspace has the same size.
concepts.L2: The point of a basis is uniqueness of representation, not minimality for its own sake. Independent + spanning is exactly the condition under which coordinates are well-defined — drop independence and a vector has many coordinate vectors, drop spanning and some vectors have none. Everything about coordinates depends on this.
concepts.L3: Uniqueness: if $x = \sum c_{i} b_{i} = \sum d_{i} b_{i}$ then $\sum (c_{i} - d_{i}) b_{i} = 0$, and independence forces $c_{i} = d_{i}$ for every i. Existence of a coordinate vector is exactly the spanning condition. Well-definedness of dimension follows from the Steinitz exchange lemma: if a set of m vectors spans S and a set of n vectors in S is independent, then $n \leq m$; applying it in both directions to two bases gives equal sizes. Standard consequences: in an n-dimensional space, any n independent vectors form a basis and any n spanning vectors form a basis — you only ever have to check one of the two conditions.

L4.prompt_tpl: Find the coordinates of x = [{x1}, {x2}] in the basis {{[1,1], [1,-1]}}.
In R^{n}, you are handed {n} vectors and told they span R^{n}. What else must you check to conclude they form a basis?
L4.answer: Nothing.
L4.explanation: In an n-dimensional space, n spanning vectors are automatically independent (and n independent vectors automatically span). Checking one condition suffices when the count matches the dimension.

L4.prompt_tpl: Is the set {{(x, y) in $\mathbb{{ R }}^{{2}} : x + y$ = {c}}} a subspace?
L4.explanation: $c=0$ contains the origin and is closed under both operations. $c=1$ fails on all three counts: (0,0) is not in it, and the sum of two solutions gives $x+y=2$.

L0.body:
A vector space over R: a set V with + : $V x V \to V$ and * : $R x V \to V$ satisfying eight axioms (associativity and commutativity of +, additive identity 0 and inverses, $1\cdot v = v, a(bv) = (ab)v$, and the two distributive laws).
Examples: $\mathbb{R}^{n}$; polynomials of degree <= n; {f : R -> R continuous}; solutions of y'' + $y = 0$.
L0.cloze: Span, {{c1::linear independence}}, {{c2::basis}}, dimension — defined by the {{c3::eight axioms}}, not by 'lists of numbers'.

concepts.L1: Span, linear independence, basis, dimension. Subspaces. The abstract definition (a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying eight axioms) rather than 'lists of numbers'.
concepts.L2: The abstraction matters because function spaces, polynomial spaces, and solution spaces of differential equations are all vector spaces. Once you see that, a lot of apparently different mathematics unifies.
concepts.L3: Every proof about span, independence, basis and dimension in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ uses only the eight axioms — never the fact that elements are tuples. So each proof transfers verbatim to any structure satisfying them. Polynomials of degree <= 2 form a 3-dimensional space with basis $\{1, x, x^{2}\}$; the coordinate map sending a + bx + $cx^{2}$ to [a,b,c] is an isomorphism onto $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, which is the general theorem: every n-dimensional real vector space is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ via a choice of basis. This is what licenses reasoning in coordinates while claiming basis-free conclusions, and why differentiation on polynomials can be written as a matrix.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that the polynomials of degree at most {n} form a vector space, and give its dimension and a basis.
L4.answer: Sums and scalar multiples of degree <= n polynomials are degree <= n; the zero polynomial is the identity; the axioms hold pointwise from R. Basis $\{1, x, \dots, x^{n}\}$; dimension $n+1$.
L4.explanation: For $n=2$ the dimension is 3. Independence: a + bx + $cx^{2} = 0$ for all x forces $a=b=c=0$ (evaluate at three points, or compare coefficients).

L4.prompt_tpl: Write differentiation $d/dx$ as a matrix on the basis $\{{1, x, x^{{2}}\}}$ of polynomials of degree <= 2, then apply it to {a} + {b}x + {c}$x^{{2}}$.
L4.explanation: $d/dx$ of $3 + 4x + 5x^{2}$ is $4 + 10x$. In coordinates $[3,4,5] \to [4,10,0]$. Note D is nilpotent $(D^{3} = 0)$, which encodes 'differentiate three times and any quadratic dies'.

L4.prompt_tpl: Is the set of solutions to {ode} a vector space? Justify from the axioms.
L4.answer: y''+$y=0$: yes (dimension 2, basis {sin x, cos x}). y''+$y=1$: no.
L4.explanation: The homogeneous equation is closed under linear combination by linearity of the derivative. The inhomogeneous one is not: if y1 and y2 both give $1, y_{1}+y_{2}$ gives 2. It is an affine set, not a subspace — the same failure as a line off the origin.

L0.body:
$T : V \to W$ is linear iff $T(x + y) = T(x) + T(y)$ and $T(cx) = c T(x)$.
Given bases, T is represented by A with columns $A[:, j] = T(e_{j})$.
np: A = np.column_stack([T(e) for e in np.eye(n)])
L0.cloze: T is linear iff {{c1::T(ax + by) = $a T(x) + b T(y)$}}; its matrix has j-th column {{c2::$T(e_{j})$}}.

concepts.L1: A linear map preserves addition and scaling, hence every linear combination. That single property forces the map to be determined entirely by what it does to a basis: know $T(e_{1})\dots T(e_{n})$ and you know T everywhere.
concepts.L2: This is where the matrix comes from, and the direction matters: you feed basis vectors in and stack the outputs as columns. Most people memorise matrix-vector multiplication first and never learn that the columns are literally the images of the basis vectors, which is why the column view later feels like a trick.
concepts.L3: Write $x = \sum_{j} x_{j} e_{j}$. Linearity gives $T(x) = T(\sum_{j} x_{j} e_{j}) = \sum_{j} x_{j} T(e_{j})$. So $T(x)$ is the linear combination of the fixed vectors $T(e_{j})$ with the coordinates of x as weights. Define A as the matrix whose j-th column is $T(e_{j})$; then $T(x) = Ax$ by definition of matrix-vector product. Conversely every matrix defines a linear map, since A(ax+by) = aAx + bAy. So linear maps between finite-dimensional spaces and matrices (given bases) are the same thing. Geometrically, linearity means grid lines stay parallel and evenly spaced and the origin stays fixed.

L4.prompt_tpl: T rotates $\mathbb{{ R }}^{{2}}$ by {deg} degrees counter-clockwise. Write its matrix by computing $T(e_{{1}})$ and $T(e_{{2}})$.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: $\cos 60 = 0.5, \sin 60 = 0.8660254$. Columns are the images of the basis vectors — that is the whole construction.

L4.prompt_tpl: Is $f(x) = Ax + b$ with b = [{b1}, {b2}] (nonzero) a linear map?
L4.answer: No.
L4.explanation: $f(0) = b \neq 0$, and any linear map sends 0 to $0 (T(0) = T(0\cdot 0) = 0\cdot T(0) = 0)$. It is affine. This is why bias terms are handled separately, or absorbed by appending a constant 1 to the input.

L4.prompt_tpl: Prove that a linear map T satisfies $T(0) = 0$.
L4.answer: $T(0) = T(0 \cdot 0) = 0 \cdot T(0) = 0$, using homogeneity with scalar 0.
L4.explanation: Trivial but load-bearing: it is the test that instantly rejects affine functions, and it is why spans and subspaces always contain the origin.

concepts.t: Matrix-vector product as a combination of columns

L0.body:
$Ax = x_{1} \cdot A[:,1] + x_{2} \cdot A[:,2] + \dots + x_{n} \cdot A[:,n]$
Row view: $(Ax)_{i} = \sum_{j} A_{ij} x_{j} = \langle \mathrm{row}_{i}(A), x\rangle$
np: A @ x  ==  sum(x[j] * A[:, j] for j in range(A.shape[1]))
L0.cloze: Ax is a {{c1::linear combination of the columns}} of A, weighted by {{c2::the entries of x}}; therefore {A x : x} is exactly the {{c3::column space}}.

concepts.L1: Ax is the linear combination of A's columns with weights x. The row-by-row dot product view gives the same numbers but hides the structure: the column view makes it immediate that the set of all Ax is the span of the columns, and that $Ax = b$ asks whether b is in that span.
concepts.L2: The row view is how you compute by hand; the column view is how you think. Nearly every confusing result — why the column space is the range, why rank bounds solvability, why a wide matrix cannot be injective — is obvious in the column view and opaque in the row view. Switch deliberately.
concepts.L3: By definition $(Ax)_{i} = \sum_{j} A_{ij} x_{j}$. Fix j and collect: the contribution of $x_{j}$ across all output coordinates i is $x_{j} \cdot [A_{1}j, \dots, A_{mj}]^{T} = x_{j} \cdot A[:,j]$. Summing over j gives $Ax = \sum_{j} x_{j} A[:,j]$. Two corollaries drop out immediately. First, range(A) = {Ax} = span of columns = $\mathrm{col}(A)$. Second, $A e_{j} = A[:,j]$, recovering 'the columns are the images of the basis vectors'. Cost: mn multiply-adds, so 2mn FLOPs, and it touches mn matrix entries — arithmetic intensity near 1, which is why GEMV is memory-bound.

L4.prompt_tpl: $A = [[2,-1,0],[1,3,4]]$, x = [{x1},{x2},{x3}]. Compute Ax by writing it as a combination of columns.
Using only the column view, explain why $Ax = b$ has a solution for every b in R^{m} only if A has at least {m} columns.
L4.answer: Ax ranges over the span of A's columns. To span R^m you need at least m vectors, so A needs at least m columns.
L4.explanation: Fewer than m columns span a subspace of dimension < m, which misses some b. This is the column view making a solvability theorem obvious in one sentence.

L4.prompt_tpl: What is A @ e_{j} where e_{j} is the {j}-th standard basis vector?
L4.answer: The j-th column of A.
L4.explanation: The combination has weight 1 on column j and 0 elsewhere. This is how you extract or define columns, and it is the bridge back to 'columns are images of basis vectors'.

L0.body:
$(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k} A_{ik} B_{kj}$.  Column view: $(AB)[:,j] = A$ @ B[:,j].  Outer-product view: AB = $\sum_{k} A[:,k] B[k,:]$.
Shapes: $(m x k)(k x n) \to (m x n)$.  $(AB)x = A(Bx)$.
np: A @ B  (never A * B, which is elementwise)
L0.cloze: AB is the matrix of {{c1::B followed by A}}; its j-th column is {{c2::A @ B[:,j]}}, and AB is defined only when {{c3::A's columns = B's rows}}.

concepts.L1: AB is the matrix of the composite map 'apply B, then A'. Three equivalent views: entry (i,j) as a dot product, column j as A applied to B's column j, and the whole product as a sum of k outer products. The last is the one that explains low-rank structure.
concepts.L2: Non-commutativity is not an algebraic quirk, it is the statement that rotating then stretching differs from stretching then rotating. And the right-to-left reading order — AB means B first — trips people forever because it fights the left-to-right habit; it comes from writing the argument on the right in $(AB)x = A(Bx)$.
concepts.L3: Define AB as the matrix representing $x \to A(Bx)$. Its j-th column is the image of $e_{j}$, which is $A(B e_{j}) = A B[:,j]$. Expanding A B[:,j] as a combination of A's columns gives $(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k} A_{ik} B_{kj}$, the entry formula. Regrouping the same double sum by k instead gives AB = sum_k A[:,k] B[k,:], a sum of k rank-1 matrices — so rank(AB) <= min(rank A, rank B), and truncating that sum is exactly what low-rank approximation does. Associativity $(AB)C = A(BC)$ is inherited from composition of functions being associative, and its cost consequences are real: for (m x k)(k x n)(n x p) the two bracketings differ in FLOP count.

L4.explanation: Verified in numpy. They differ, which is the generic case: matrix multiplication does not commute because composition of maps does not.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must compute A B C with shapes A: {m}x{k}, B: {k}x{n}, C: {n}x{p}. Which bracketing is cheaper, and by how many FLOPs (count 2*rows*inner*cols per product)? Answer with the FLOP count of the cheaper bracketing.
L4.answer: (AB)C costs $2\cdot 1000\cdot 10\cdot 1000 + 2\cdot 1000\cdot 1000\cdot 10 = 40,000,000 \mathrm{FLOPs}$. $A(BC)$ costs $2\cdot 10\cdot 1000\cdot 10 + 2\cdot 1000\cdot 10\cdot 10 = 400,000 \mathrm{FLOPs}$. $A(BC)$ is 100x cheaper.
L4.explanation: Verified: $2\cdot 1e3\cdot 1e1\cdot 1e3 = 2e7$ twice = 4e7; versus $2\cdot 1e1\cdot 1e3\cdot 1e1 = 2e5$ plus $2\cdot 1e3\cdot 1e1\cdot 1e1 = 2e5$, total 4e5. Associativity is free mathematically and expensive to get wrong computationally — this is exactly the LoRA ordering argument.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that rank(AB) <= min(rank A, rank B) using the outer-product view.
L4.answer: AB = sum_{k} A[:,k] B[k,:], a sum of at most k rank-1 terms; also every column of AB lies in $\mathrm{col}(A)$ and every row lies in $\mathrm{row}(B)$.
L4.explanation: $\mathrm{col}(AB)$ is a subspace of $\mathrm{col}(A)$ since each column of AB is A times something; symmetrically for rows. Hence the rank cannot exceed either factor's rank.

prereqs: Matrix-vector product as a combination of columns

L0.body:
A represents T in a chosen basis: A[:,j] = coordinates of $T(b_{j})$.
Change of basis: if P has the new basis vectors as columns, the same map is $P^{-1} A P$ in the new basis.
np: np.linalg.inv(P) @ A @ P
L0.cloze: Matrix multiplication is {{c1::composition of maps}}; change of basis is {{c2::$P^{-1} A P$}}.

concepts.L1: A matrix is a linear map expressed in a chosen basis, not a grid of numbers. Matrix multiplication is composition of maps. Change of basis is P⁻¹AP.
concepts.L2: This single reframe is the difference between deep learning looking like notation and looking like geometry. If matrix multiplication still feels like an arbitrary rule, stop and fix this before continuing.
concepts.L3: Let P have the new basis vectors as columns, so P maps new-basis coordinates to old-basis coordinates. To apply T to a vector given in new coordinates: convert to old (P), apply the map (A), convert back $(P^{-1})$. Composing right-to-left gives $P^{-1} A P$. Two matrices related this way are called similar, and similarity is an equivalence relation whose classes are exactly 'the same map, different bases'. Everything invariant under it — trace, determinant, eigenvalues, rank, characteristic polynomial — is a property of the map itself; anything that changes, such as individual entries or whether the matrix is symmetric, is an artefact of the basis.

L4.prompt_tpl: $A = [[3,1],[0,2]], P = [[1,1],[0,1]]$. Compute $P^{{-1}} A P$, and verify the trace and determinant are unchanged.
L4.answer: $P^{-1}AP = [[3, 2], [0, 2]]; \mathrm{trace} 5$ and determinant 6 in both.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: $P^{-1}AP = [[3,2],[0,2]]$. $\mathrm{trace}(A) = 5 = \mathrm{trace}(P^{-1}AP); \det = 6$ in both; eigenvalues {3,2} in both. Entries changed, invariants did not.

L4.prompt_tpl: A map has matrix A in one basis and D = diag({d1}, {d2}) in another. What does that say about the map?
L4.answer: In that basis the map is pure independent scaling along the basis directions: it scales one axis by 3 and the other by 2. Those directions are eigenvectors and the diagonal entries are eigenvalues.
L4.explanation: Diagonal in some basis = diagonalizable. The complicated-looking A and the trivial D are the same geometric action described in different coordinates.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these are invariant under similarity: (a) trace, (b) the entry $A_{{11}}, (c)$ eigenvalues, (d) symmetry of the matrix?
L4.answer: (a) and (c).
L4.explanation: Trace and eigenvalues (and determinant, rank, characteristic polynomial) are properties of the map. Individual entries and symmetry depend on the basis — symmetry is only basis-independent if you restrict to orthonormal changes of basis.

L0.body:
$(A^{T})_{ij} = A_{ji}$.  $(AB)^{T} = B^{T} A^{T}$.  $(A^{T})^{T} = A$.
Defining property: $\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, A^{T} y\rangle$ for all x, y.
np: A.T ; A.transpose() ; torch: A.mT (batched)
L0.cloze: $(AB)^{T}$ = {{c1::$B^{T} A^{T}$}} — the order {{c2::reverses}}; and $\langle Ax, y\rangle$ = {{c3::$\langle x, A^{T} y\rangle$}}.

concepts.L1: The transpose swaps rows and columns, but its real definition is the adjoint property $\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, A^{T} y\rangle : A^{T}$ is the unique matrix that lets you move A across an inner product. Products reverse order under transposition.
concepts.L2: Treating the transpose as a formatting operation is why gradient derivations go wrong. It is the map that turns a question about outputs into a question about inputs — which is exactly what backpropagation does, and why the backward pass of $y = Wx$ is $W^{T}$ times the incoming gradient rather than W.
concepts.L3: Adjoint property: $\langle Ax, y\rangle = (Ax)^{T} y = x^{T} A^{T} y = \langle x, A^{T} y\rangle$, using only associativity and $(AB)^{T} = B^{T} A^{T}$. The reversal rule itself: $((AB)^{T})_{ij} = (AB)_{ji} = \sum_{k} A_{jk} B_{ki} = \sum_{k} (B^{T})_{ik} (A^{T})_{kj} = (B^{T} A^{T})_{ij}$. Shape-checking makes it memorable — if A is m x k and B is k x n then $B^{T} A^{T}$ is n x k times $k x m = n x m$, which is the only order that type-checks. In backprop, if $y = Wx$ then $dL/dx = W^{T} (dL/dy)$, which is the adjoint statement: the sensitivity of the loss to inputs is $A^{T}$ applied to the sensitivity to outputs.

L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: both equal [[4,10],[5,11]]. The order reversal is forced by shapes: $B^{T} A^{T}$ is $(2\times 3)$ times $(3\times 2)$, the only product of the two transposes that type-checks.

L4.prompt_tpl: A is {m}x{n}. What are the shapes of $A^{{ T }} A$ and $A A^{{ T }}$?
L4.answer: $A^{T} A$ is $n x n; A A^{T}$ is m x m. Both are symmetric and positive semidefinite.
L4.explanation: For $m=5, n=3: A^{T} A$ is $3x_{3}, A A^{T}$ is 5x5. Symmetry: $(A^{T} A)^{T} = A^{T} (A^{T})^{T} = A^{T} A$. PSD: $x^{T} A^{T} A x = \|Ax\|^{2} \geq 0$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given $y = Wx$ and a scalar loss L, derive $dL/dx$ in terms of W and $dL/dy$.
L4.answer: $dL/dx = W^{T} (dL/dy)$.
L4.explanation: By the chain rule $dL/dx_{j} = \sum_{i} (dL/dy_{i})(dy_{i}/dx_{j}) = \sum_{i} (dL/dy_{i}) W_{ij} = (W^{T} dL/dy)_{j}$. The transpose appears because the Jacobian of y w.r.t. x is W and reverse-mode applies its adjoint.

L0.cloze: A is invertible iff {{c1::$\det (A) \neq 0$}} iff $\mathrm{rank} = n$ iff {{c2::$\mathrm{null}(A) = \{0\}$}}; and $(AB)^{-1}$ = {{c3::$B^{-1} A^{-1}$}}.

concepts.L1: $A^{-1}$ undoes A. It exists exactly when A is square and its columns are independent — equivalently nonzero determinant, full rank, trivial null space, all eigenvalues nonzero. Inverses reverse under products because undoing a composition means undoing the last step first.
concepts.L2: Never form an explicit inverse to solve $Ax = b$. np.linalg.solve does an LU factorisation: roughly 3x fewer FLOPs than inverting, and numerically more accurate. Explicit inverses in production numerical code are almost always a bug or a performance leak; the notation $A^{-1}b$ means 'solve', not 'invert then multiply'.
concepts.L3: Uniqueness: if BA = I = AC then $B = B(AC) = (BA)C = C$. Existence is equivalent to bijectivity of $x \to Ax$, which for square A is equivalent to injectivity $(\mathrm{null}(A) = \{0\})$, which is equivalent to independent columns, full rank n, and det != 0 — the invertible matrix theorem, all one condition wearing different clothes. Reversal: $(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1}) = A(BB^{-1})A^{-1} = I$. Cost: LU factorisation is about $(2/3)n^{3} \mathrm{FLOPs}$ and then two triangular solves at $n^{2}$ each; explicit inversion is about $2n^{3}$ and then a matvec, and it loses accuracy by squaring nothing useful while adding rounding.

L4.prompt_tpl: Invert $A = [[4,7],[2,6]]$ by the 2x2 formula.
You need to solve $A x = b$ for {k} different right-hand sides b, with A fixed and {n}x{n}. Compute $A^{{-1}}$ once and multiply, or factor once and back-substitute?
L4.answer: Factor once (LU), then two triangular solves per right-hand side. Cheaper and more accurate than explicit inversion.
L4.explanation: LU is ~$(2/3)n^{3}$ once, then $2n^{2}$ per RHS; inversion is ~$2n^{3}$ plus $2n^{2}$ per RHS. The factorisation also avoids the extra rounding error that forming the inverse introduces. numpy: scipy.linalg.lu_factor / lu_solve.

L4.prompt_tpl: A is {n}x{n} with rank {r}. Is A invertible?
options: Only if A is also symmetric
L4.answer: Invertible iff $r = n$; otherwise not.
L4.explanation: Rank deficiency means dependent columns, a nontrivial null vector, zero determinant, and a non-injective map — no inverse can exist.

L0.body:
Row ops: swap, scale, add a multiple of one row to another. Reduce $[A | b]$ to upper triangular, then back-substitute.
A = LU (or PA = LU with partial pivoting), L unit lower triangular, U upper triangular.
scipy.linalg.lu_factor(A); scipy.linalg.lu_solve(lu, b)
L0.cloze: Elimination costs about {{c1::$(2/3)n^{3}$}} FLOPs and records its multipliers in {{c2::L}}; pivoting is needed for {{c3::numerical stability}}, not just for zero pivots.

concepts.L1: Elimination systematically zeroes below each pivot to reach an upper-triangular system solvable by back-substitution. The multipliers you used are exactly the entries of L, so the same work produces the factorization A = LU — the standard workhorse for solving square systems.
concepts.L2: Partial pivoting is not only for zero pivots. A merely small pivot makes the multipliers huge and amplifies rounding catastrophically, so you swap to the largest available pivot every time even when nothing is zero. This is the first place where 'mathematically equivalent' and 'numerically equivalent' come apart.
concepts.L3: Each elimination step subtracting m times row k from row i is left-multiplication by an elementary matrix $\mathbb{E}_{ik}(-m)$; the product of all of them is unit lower triangular with the multipliers in place, and its inverse is L with the multipliers unnegated — which is why L is free. Cost: eliminating column k touches an (n-k) x (n-k) submatrix, giving $\sum_{k} 2(n-k)^{2} \approx (2/3)n^{3} \mathrm{FLOPs}$, then $n^{2}$ for each triangular solve. With partial pivoting the multipliers satisfy $|m| \leq 1$, bounding growth; PA = LU. Backward error analysis says the computed solution exactly solves a nearby system $(A + dA)x = b$ with $\|dA\|$ small relative to the growth factor.

L4.prompt_tpl: Solve by elimination: $2x + y + z = 5, 4x - 6y = -2, -2x + 7y + 2z = 9$.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: np.linalg.solve([[2,1,1],[4,-6,0],[-2,7,2]], [5,-2,9]) = [1,1,2]. Elimination reaches this in two passes with no pivoting needed here, and the LU factors are reusable if only the right-hand side changes.

L4.prompt_tpl: Roughly how many FLOPs does LU factorization of an {n}x{n} matrix cost, and how many does each subsequent solve cost? Answer with the LU factorization FLOP count.
L4.answer: $n=1000$: LU ~ $(2/3)(1e9) \approx 6.67e8 \mathrm{FLOPs}$; each solve ~ $2n^{2} = 2e6 \mathrm{FLOPs}$.
L4.explanation: $(2/3)n^{3}$ for the factorization, $2 \cdot n^{2}$ for forward + back substitution. The ratio $n/3$ is why you factor once and reuse.

L4.prompt_tpl: The pivot in column 1 is {p} and another row has entry 1 in that column. Why swap even though {p} is nonzero?
L4.answer: The multipliers would be about $1/p$, enormous, so rounding errors in the pivot row get amplified by that factor into the rest of the matrix. Swapping to the largest pivot keeps all multipliers at most 1.
L4.explanation: Classic demonstration: solving with the tiny pivot in floating point loses most significant digits; with the swap the same system solves accurately. This is stability, not correctness — both are exact in exact arithmetic.

L0.body:
$\mathrm{rank}(A) = \dim (\mathrm{col}(A)) = \dim (\mathrm{row}(A))$ = number of pivots in the row echelon form = number of nonzero singular values.
rank(AB) <= min(rank A, rank B).  $\mathrm{rank}(A) \leq \min (m, n)$.
np.linalg.matrix_rank(A)   # SVD-based, with a tolerance
L0.cloze: Row rank {{c1::equals}} column rank; rank is the number of {{c2::pivots}}, and numerically the number of singular values above a {{c3::tolerance}}.

concepts.L1: Rank is the number of genuinely independent directions a matrix has — the dimension of its column space, which provably equals the dimension of its row space. It is the size of the output space the map can actually reach, and it caps how much information the map preserves.
concepts.L2: Rank is discontinuous and therefore fictional in floating point: a rank-2 matrix plus 1e-16 of noise has rank 3 exactly. numpy.linalg.matrix_rank counts singular values above a tolerance for this reason. In practice 'rank' means 'numerical rank', and the honest object is the singular value spectrum, not an integer.
concepts.L3: Row rank = column rank: reduce A to row echelon form by invertible row operations, which change neither the row space nor the dependency relations among columns. The nonzero rows of the echelon form are independent and span the row space; the pivot columns are independent and span the column space; both counts equal the number of pivots. Alternatively, write A = CR where C holds independent columns and R the coefficients: the columns of A are combinations of r columns of C, and the rows are combinations of r rows of R, so both ranks equal r. rank(AB) <= min(rank A, rank B) because $\mathrm{col}(AB)$ is a subspace of $\mathrm{col}(A)$ and $\mathrm{row}(AB)$ is a subspace of $\mathrm{row}(B)$.

L4.explanation: Row $2 = 2 \cdot \mathrm{row} 1$, so only two independent rows remain. Verified: np.linalg.matrix_rank = 2.

L4.prompt_tpl: A is {m}x{n} with rank {r}. B is {n}x{p}. What is the maximum possible rank of AB?
L4.explanation: $\mathrm{rank}(AB) \leq \min (\mathrm{rank} A, \mathrm{rank} B) \leq \mathrm{rank} A = 2$. This is exactly the LoRA argument: a product through a narrow bottleneck cannot exceed the bottleneck's rank.

L4.prompt_tpl: A truly rank-{r} matrix is stored in float32 and read back. np.linalg.matrix_rank returns {rp}. Explain and say what to report instead.
L4.answer: Rounding perturbs the exactly-zero singular values to tiny nonzero values, so the exact rank jumps. Report the singular value spectrum, or the rank at an explicit tolerance.
L4.explanation: Rank is not continuous in the entries; the singular values are. Any pipeline that branches on an exact rank is fragile.

L0.body:
For A of shape $m x n: \mathrm{rank}(A) + \dim (\mathrm{null}(A)) = n$.
$\mathrm{null}(A) = \{x : Ax = 0\}$.  nullity = number of free (non-pivot) columns.
scipy.linalg.null_space(A)
L0.cloze: $\mathrm{rank}(A) + \mathrm{nullity}(A)$ = {{c1::n}}, the number of {{c2::columns}} — pivot columns count toward {{c3::rank}}, free columns toward nullity.

concepts.L1: Every input dimension is either preserved or destroyed: rank counts the directions that survive, nullity counts the directions collapsed to zero, and they sum to the number of columns. In echelon form, pivot columns are the survivors and free columns the casualties.
concepts.L2: The n on the right is the number of columns, not rows — a common and expensive slip when the matrix is not square. Consequence worth internalising: a wide matrix $(n > m)$ always has a nontrivial null space, so any layer that reduces dimension is irreversibly lossy, no matter what the weights are.
concepts.L3: Take a basis $\{u_{1}\dots u_{k}\}$ of $\mathrm{null}(A)$ and extend it to a basis $\{u_{1}\dots u_{k}, w_{1}\dots w_{r}\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, so $k + r = n$. Claim: $\{A w_{1}\dots A w_{r}\}$ is a basis of $\mathrm{col}(A)$. Spanning: any Ax expands x in the full basis, and the u terms map to zero. Independence: if $\sum c_{i} A w_{i} = 0$ then sum c_i w_i is in $\mathrm{null}(A)$, hence a combination of the u's; but the full set is independent, so all $c_{i} = 0$. Therefore $\mathrm{rank} = r$ and $\mathrm{nullity} = k$, giving $r + k = n$. The theorem is the first-isomorphism theorem for vector spaces in disguise: $\mathbb{R}^{n} / \mathrm{null}(A)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{col}(A)$.

L4.prompt_tpl: A is {m}x{n} with rank {r}. What is $\dim (\mathrm{{ null }}(A))$?
L4.explanation: $\mathrm{nullity} = n - \mathrm{rank} = 5 - 2 = 3$. Note it depends on the number of columns, not rows.

L4.prompt_tpl: A linear layer maps R^{n} -> R^{m} with $n > m$. Can it be injective?
options: Only if the layer also has a bias term
L4.answer: No.
L4.explanation: rank <= m < n, so $\mathrm{nullity} = n - \mathrm{rank} \geq n - m > 0$. A nonzero null vector means two distinct inputs share an output. Dimension reduction is always lossy; no choice of weights avoids it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Use rank-nullity to show that a square matrix is injective iff it is surjective.
L4.answer: For n x n: injective iff nullity 0 iff rank n iff $\mathrm{col}(A) = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ iff surjective.
L4.explanation: The equivalence fails for non-square matrices, which is why 'left inverse' and 'right inverse' separate there. This is one line of the invertible matrix theorem.

$\langle x, y\rangle = x^{T} y = \sum_{i} x_{i} y_{i} = \|x\| \|y\| \cos (\theta)$.
x perp y iff $x^{T} y = 0$.  Cauchy-Schwarz: $|x^{T} y| \leq \|x\| \|y\|$.
$\cos_{\mathrm{sim}} = x$ @ y / (np.linalg.norm(x) * np.linalg.norm(y))
L0.cloze: $x^{T} y$ = {{c1::$\|x\| \|y\| \cos (\theta)$}}; orthogonal means {{c2::$x^{T} y = 0$}}; and $|x^{T} y| \leq \|x\| \|y\|$ is {{c3::Cauchy-Schwarz}}.

concepts.L1: The dot product measures alignment: it is the product of lengths times the cosine of the angle between them. Zero means perpendicular. It is the single operation from which length, angle, projection, and orthogonality are all defined.
concepts.L2: Cosine similarity is the dot product with lengths divided out, which is why embedding norms silently stop mattering the moment you normalise — and why a model can encode magnitude information that your retrieval metric then discards. Choosing dot product versus cosine is a modelling decision, not a formatting one.
concepts.L3: Start from the law of cosines on the triangle with sides $x, y, x - y: \|x-y\|^{2} = \|x\|^{2} + \|y\|^{2} - 2\|x\|\|y\|\cos (\theta)$. Expanding the left side algebraically gives $\|x\|^{2} - 2x^{T} y + \|y\|^{2}$. Equating yields $x^{T} y = \|x\|\|y\|\cos (\theta)$, so the algebraic definition and the geometric one agree, and orthogonality ($\theta = 90$ degrees) is exactly $x^{T} y = 0$. Cauchy-Schwarz follows since |cos| <= 1; a purely algebraic proof considers the quadratic $q(t) = \|x + t y\|^{2} \geq 0$, whose nonpositive discriminant is $(x^{T} y)^{2} - \|x\|^{2}\|y\|^{2} \leq 0$. The triangle inequality follows from Cauchy-Schwarz.

L4.prompt_tpl: $a = [1,2,2], b = [3,0,4]$. Compute $a^{{ T }} b$ and $\cos (\theta)$. Answer with cos(theta).
Prove Cauchy-Schwarz from the fact that $\|x + t y\|^{{2}} \geq 0$ for all real t.
L4.answer: Expand: $\|y\|^{2} t^{2} + 2(x^{T} y)t + \|x\|^{2} \geq 0$. A nonnegative quadratic has discriminant <= $0: 4(x^{T} y)^{2} - 4\|x\|^{2}\|y\|^{2} \leq 0$, giving $|x^{T} y| \leq \|x\| \|y\|$.
L4.explanation: No geometry needed, so the proof works in any inner product space — including function spaces, where it gives the integral form.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two embeddings have cosine similarity {c} but very different norms. For a retrieval system, does dot-product or cosine ranking treat them differently, and which should you use?
L4.answer: Dot product ranks the larger-norm vector higher; cosine ranks them identically. Use cosine when norm encodes nothing you want (e.g. token frequency artefacts), dot product when norm encodes confidence or relevance you want to keep.
L4.explanation: The choice changes results materially. Many embedding models are trained with one of the two objectives, and mismatching train and inference metrics is a common silent bug.

L0.body:
$\mathrm{col}(A)$ subset R^m, dim r.  $\mathrm{null}(A^{T})$ subset R^m, dim m - r.  $\mathrm{row}(A)$ subset R^n, dim r.  $\mathrm{null}(A)$ subset R^n, dim n - r.
$\mathrm{col}(A) \perp \mathrm{null}(A^{T}); \mathrm{row}(A) \perp \mathrm{null}(A)$.
scipy.linalg.null_space(A), scipy.linalg.orth(A)
L0.cloze: rank + nullity = {{c1::number of columns}}; row rank {{c2::equals}} column rank; col(A) is orthogonal to {{c3::$\mathrm{null}(A^{T})$}}.

concepts.L1: Column space and left null space in the output space; row space and null space in the input space. Rank-nullity: rank + nullity = number of columns. Row rank equals column rank.
concepts.L2: Strang builds his entire course around this and it's the right organizing frame. Rank as 'the dimension of the information the map preserves' is the intuition worth carrying.
concepts.L3: Orthogonality: x is in $\mathrm{null}(A)$ iff $Ax = 0$ iff every row of A dots to zero with x iff x is orthogonal to $\mathrm{row}(A)$. So $\mathrm{null}(A) = \mathrm{row}(A)^{\perp}$ inside $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, and dimensions $r + (n-r) = n$ confirm they are complements. Applying the same argument to $A^{T}$ gives $\mathrm{null}(A^{T}) = \mathrm{col}(A)^{\perp}$ inside $\mathbb{R}^{m}$. The picture: A maps $\mathrm{row}(A)$ bijectively onto $\mathrm{col}(A)$, kills $\mathrm{null}(A)$ entirely, and reaches nothing in $\mathrm{null}(A^{T})$. $Ax = b$ is solvable iff b is in $\mathrm{col}(A)$ iff b is orthogonal to every solution of $A^{T} y = 0$ — the Fredholm alternative.

L4.prompt_tpl: A is {m}x{n} with rank {r}. Give the dimensions of all four fundamental subspaces and say which ambient space each lives in.
L4.answer: col(A): dim 2 in $\mathbb{R}^{5}$. null(A^T): dim 3 in $\mathbb{R}^{5}$. row(A): dim 2 in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. null(A): dim 1 in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$.
L4.explanation: $r = 2; m - r = 3; n - r = 1$. The two output-space subspaces sum to 5, the two input-space subspaces sum to 3.

L4.prompt_tpl: $A^{{ T }} y = 0$ has a nonzero solution y, and $y^{{ T }} b$ = {v} != 0. Is $Ax = b$ solvable?
L4.answer: No.
L4.explanation: Solvability requires b in $\mathrm{col}(A) = \mathrm{null}(A^{T})^{\perp}$, so b must be orthogonal to every left null vector. A nonzero $y^{T} b$ certifies inconsistency — the Fredholm alternative, and the cheapest possible proof that a system has no solution.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that $\mathrm{{ null }}(A)$ is orthogonal to $\mathrm{{ row }}(A)$.
L4.answer: $Ax = 0$ means every row of A has zero dot product with x; a vector orthogonal to each row is orthogonal to their span, which is $\mathrm{row}(A)$.
L4.explanation: Both directions hold, so $\mathrm{null}(A)$ is exactly $\mathrm{row}(A)^{\perp}$, not merely contained in it — the dimension count $r + (n-r) = n$ confirms equality.

concepts.t: Solving Ax = b: existence and uniqueness

L0.body:
Existence: b in $\mathrm{col}(A)$.  Uniqueness: $\mathrm{null}(A) = \{0\}$.
General solution = one particular solution + any null-space vector: $x = x_{p} + x_{n}$.
np.linalg.solve (square, nonsingular); np.linalg.lstsq (general)
L0.cloze: Solutions are {{c1::$x_{p} + \mathrm{null}(A)$}}: an affine set. Zero, one, or {{c2::infinitely many}} solutions — never exactly {{c3::two}}.

concepts.L1: Existence and uniqueness are separate questions with separate answers: existence asks whether b lies in the column space, uniqueness asks whether the null space is trivial. The full solution set is one particular solution translated by the entire null space.
concepts.L2: A real linear system has zero, one, or infinitely many solutions — never exactly seven. That follows from the solution set being an affine translate of a subspace, and it is the fastest sanity check on any claim about a linear model's identifiability.
concepts.L3: If $Ax_{p} = b$ and $Ax = b$ then $A(x - x_{p}) = 0$, so $x - x_{p}$ is in $\mathrm{null}(A)$ and x lies in $x_{p} + \mathrm{null}(A)$. Conversely every such x satisfies $A(x_{p} + n) = b + 0 = b$. So the solution set is empty (b not in $\mathrm{col}(A)$) or a coset of $\mathrm{null}(A)$, whose cardinality is 1 if $\mathrm{null}(A) = \{0\}$ and infinite otherwise, since a subspace with a nonzero vector contains its whole line. The four cases by shape: full column rank and b in $\mathrm{col}(A)$ gives a unique solution; full row rank always gives at least one; both gives exactly one (square invertible); neither gives either none or infinitely many.

L4.prompt_tpl: A is {m}x{n} with rank {r}, and b is in $\mathrm{{ col }}(A)$. How many solutions does $Ax = b$ have?
L4.answer: Infinitely many — an affine set of dimension $n - r = 2$.
L4.explanation: Existence holds by assumption; $\mathrm{nullity} = 5 - 3 = 2 > 0$ destroys uniqueness. The solution set is a 2-dimensional plane in $\mathbb{R}^{5}$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Someone reports that a linear system has exactly {k} distinct solutions. What do you conclude?
L4.answer: They are wrong.
L4.explanation: Over R the solution set is empty or an affine subspace, so its size is 0, 1, or infinite. Two distinct solutions generate a whole line of them.

L4.prompt_tpl: $x_{{ p }}$ = [1, 0, {c}] solves $Ax = b$, and $\mathrm{{ null }}(A) = \mathrm{{ span }}\{{[1,-1,0]\}}$. Write the general solution.
L4.explanation: Particular plus homogeneous. Every solution has this form and every t gives a solution. The solution set is a coset of $\mathrm{null}(A)$ — an affine subspace of dimension equal to the nullity, and a subspace only when $b = 0$.

$\det (A)$ = the signed volume scaling factor of the map $x \to Ax$.
$\det (AB) = \det (A)\det (B); \det (A^{T}) = \det (A); \det (A^{-1}) = 1/\det (A); \det (cA) = c^{n} \det (A)$.
2x2: ad - bc.  $\det (A)$ = product of eigenvalues = product of pivots.
np.linalg.det(A) ; np.linalg.slogdet(A)   # use slogdet in practice
L0.cloze: $|\det (A)|$ is the factor by which A scales {{c1::volume}}; the sign records {{c2::orientation}}; $\det = 0$ iff the map {{c3::collapses}} a dimension.

concepts.L1: The determinant is the factor by which a map scales volume, with a sign recording whether orientation flips. Zero determinant means the unit cube is flattened into something lower-dimensional, which is exactly rank deficiency, dependent columns, and non-invertibility.
concepts.L2: Multiplicativity $\det (AB) = \det (A)\det (B)$ is obvious from the volume view and a slog from the cofactor formula. Also: cofactor expansion is $O(n!)$ and never used — determinants come from LU pivots, and you want slogdet, because det underflows long before a large matrix is anywhere near singular.
concepts.L3: Characterise det as the unique function of the columns that is multilinear, alternating (zero if two columns are equal), and equal to 1 on the identity. Signed volume satisfies all three: scaling one edge scales the volume, a degenerate parallelepiped has zero volume, and the unit cube has volume 1. Uniqueness then forces the familiar formulas. Multiplicativity: applying B then A scales volume by $\det (B)$ then $\det (A)$. Zero determinant means the image of the unit cube is flat, i.e. the columns are dependent, i.e. some direction is collapsed — connecting to $\mathrm{null}(A) \neq \{0\}$. Computationally, elimination gives $\det = (-1)^{swaps}$ * product of pivots, at $(2/3)n^{3}$.

L4.explanation: Expanding: $2(12-2) - 0(4-2) + 1(1-3) = 20 - 0 - 2 = 18$. Verified in numpy: 18.0. A nonzero determinant says the columns are independent; the unit cube maps to a parallelepiped of volume 18 with orientation preserved.

L4.prompt_tpl: A is {n}x{n} with $\det (A)$ = {d}. What is det({c}A), and what happens to the volume of a unit cube under A? Answer with det(cA).
L4.answer: $\det (2A) = 2^{3} \cdot 2 = 16$; the unit cube's image has volume $|\det A| = 2$.
L4.explanation: Scaling all n columns by c scales volume by $c^{n}$. Verified: for $n=3, c=2, \det =2, \det (cA) = 8\cdot 2 = 16$.

L4.prompt_tpl: You compute the log-likelihood of a Gaussian with a {n}x{n} covariance and np.linalg.det returns 0.0. Diagnose and fix.
L4.answer: Underflow, not singularity: the product of n positive but sub-unit eigenvalues falls below the smallest representable float. Use np.linalg.slogdet, or sum the logs of the Cholesky diagonal times 2.
L4.explanation: $\log \det = 2 \cdot \sum (\log (\mathrm{diag}(L)))$ for $A = LL^{T}$. Determinants of large matrices should essentially never be formed directly; you almost always want the log.

L0.body:
$\|x\|_{1} = \sum |x_{i}|; \|x\|_{2} = \sqrt{\sum x_{i}^{2}}; \|x\|_{\infty} = \max |x_{i}|$.
Frobenius: $\|A\|_{F} = \sqrt{\sum A_{ij}^{2}} = \sqrt{\sum \sigma_{i}^{2}}$.
Spectral (operator 2-norm): $\|A\|_{2} = \max_{x \neq 0} \|Ax\|/\|x\| = \sigma_{\max}$.
np.linalg.norm(x, ord) ; np.linalg.norm(A, 2) vs np.linalg.norm(A, 'fro')
L0.cloze: The spectral norm equals {{c1::$\sigma_{\max}$}}; the Frobenius norm equals {{c2::$\sqrt{\sum \sigma_{i}^{2}}$}}; a norm requires {{c3::the triangle inequality}}, homogeneity, and positivity.

concepts.L1: A norm assigns length: positive except at zero, homogeneous, and satisfying the triangle inequality. For matrices the crucial distinction is between entrywise norms (Frobenius) and operator norms (spectral), which answers 'how much can this map stretch any vector?'.
concepts.L2: np.linalg.norm(A) defaults to Frobenius, not spectral — a real source of wrong answers when you meant the operator norm. Frobenius is cheap; spectral costs an SVD but is the one bounding $\|Ax\| \leq \|A\|_{2}\|x\|$, so it is what gradient clipping and spectral normalisation actually need.
concepts.L3: All norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent up to constants ($\|x\|_{\infty} \leq \|x\|_{2} \leq \|x\|_{1} \leq \sqrt{n}\|x\|_{2}$, and so on), so convergence questions do not depend on the choice — but constants do, and constants are what stability bounds are made of. The spectral norm: $\|Ax\|^{2} = x^{T} A^{T} A x$ is maximised over unit x by the top eigenvector of $A^{T} A$, with value $\lambda_{\max}(A^{T} A) = \sigma_{\max}^{2}$, so $\|A\|_{2} = \sigma_{\max}$. Frobenius: ||A||_F^2 = trace(A^T A) = sum of eigenvalues of $A^{T} A = \sum \sigma_{i}^{2}$. Hence $\|A\|_{2} \leq \|A\|_{F} \leq \sqrt{r}\|A\|_{2}$ for rank r, and the two coincide exactly when A is rank 1.

L4.prompt_tpl: For $w = [3, -4, 12]$, compute the 1-, 2- and infinity-norms.
L4.explanation: $3+4+12 = 19; \sqrt{9+16+144} = \sqrt{169} = 13; \max = 12$. Verified in numpy. The ordering $\|w\|_{\infty} \leq \|w\|_{2} \leq \|w\|_{1}$ always holds, and the size of the gaps is what regularisation choices exploit.

L4.prompt_tpl: $A = [[3,0],[4,5]]$. Compute the Frobenius norm and the spectral norm.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: svals = $[6.708204, 2.236068]; \sqrt{6.708204^{2} + 2.236068^{2}} = 7.071068 = \sqrt{50}$. The two norms differ by ~5% here and can differ by $\sqrt{r}$ in general.

L4.prompt_tpl: You want to bound how much a layer can amplify an input perturbation of size {eps}. Which matrix norm do you need, and what is the bound?
L4.answer: The spectral norm: ||A dx||_2 <= ||A||_2 * ||dx||_2 = sigma_max * eps.
L4.explanation: Frobenius also gives a valid but looser bound since $\|A\|_{F} \geq \|A\|_{2}$. Lipschitz constants of linear layers are spectral norms, which is what spectral normalisation controls.

$Q^{T} Q = I$, so $Q^{-1} = Q^{T}$.  Columns are orthonormal.
$\|Qx\| = \|x\|; (Qx)^{T}(Qy) = x^{T} y; |\det Q| = 1$;  all |eigenvalues$| = 1; \mathrm{cond}_{2}(Q) = 1$.
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A)
L0.cloze: Q is orthogonal iff {{c1::$Q^{T} Q = I$}}, hence $Q^{-1}$ = {{c2::$Q^{T}$}}; orthogonal maps preserve {{c3::lengths and angles}}.

concepts.L1: An orthogonal matrix has orthonormal columns, so its inverse is its transpose. Geometrically it is a rotation or reflection: lengths, angles and volumes are preserved. Its condition number is exactly 1, which makes it the numerically safest object in the subject.
concepts.L2: The reason QR beats the normal equations for least squares is entirely here: multiplying by an orthogonal matrix cannot amplify error, because $\mathrm{cond}(Q) = 1$. Every stable algorithm in numerical linear algebra is built out of orthogonal transformations (Householder, Givens) for exactly this reason.
concepts.L3: $Q^{T} Q = I$ says column i dotted with column j is $\delta_{ij}$ — orthonormality. Length preservation: $\|Qx\|^{2} = x^{T} Q^{T} Q x = x^{T} x = \|x\|^{2}$. Angle preservation follows since inner products are preserved. Determinant: $\det (Q)^{2} = \det (Q^{T} Q) = \det (I) = 1$, so $\det Q = +/-1$ (+1 rotation, -1 reflection). Eigenvalues have modulus 1 since $|\lambda | \|v\| = \|Qv\| = \|v\|$. Condition number $\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min} = 1/1 = 1$, so relative errors pass through unamplified. Products of orthogonal matrices are orthogonal, which is why algorithms compose many small reflections.

L4.prompt_tpl: Q is the rotation by {deg} degrees. Verify $Q^{{ T }} Q = I$ and compute Q @ [1, 0].
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: Q.T @ $Q = I$ to machine precision, $\det = 1.0$, and the image of e1 is the unit vector at 60 degrees.

L4.prompt_tpl: What is the condition number (2-norm) of an orthogonal {n}x{n} matrix?
L4.answer: Exactly 1.
L4.explanation: All singular values are 1, so $\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min} = 1$. No other class of matrices is guaranteed this, and it is why orthogonal transformations are the building blocks of stable algorithms.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain, using $\mathrm{{ cond }}(Q) = 1$, why solving least squares via QR is more accurate than via the normal equations $A^{{ T }} A x = A^{{ T }} b$.
L4.answer: Forming $A^{T} A$ squares the condition number $(\mathrm{cond}(A^{T} A) = \mathrm{cond}(A)^{2})$, so error is amplified quadratically. QR applies only orthogonal transformations, which do not amplify error at all, leaving the sensitivity at $\mathrm{cond}(A)$.
L4.explanation: Verified example: $A = \mathrm{diag}(3, 1)$ has $\mathrm{cond} 3, A^{T} A = \mathrm{diag}(9, 1)$ has cond 9. For an ill-conditioned A this is the difference between a usable answer and noise.

Projection onto a line: $P = a a^{T} / (a^{T} a)$.  Onto $\mathrm{col}(A): P = A(A^{T} A)^{-1} A^{T}$.
$P^{2} = P, P^{T} = P$.  Residual b - Pb is orthogonal to $\mathrm{col}(A)$.
Gram-Schmidt -> A = QR; least squares via $Q^{T} b$ then back-substitute $R x = Q^{T} b$.
L0.cloze: P = {{c1::$A(A^{T} A)^{-1} A^{T}$}}; a projection satisfies {{c2::$P^{2} = P$}} and $P^{T} = P$; least squares is projection onto {{c3::the column space}}.

concepts.L1: Orthogonal complements, Gram-Schmidt, QR decomposition, projection matrices P = A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ. Least squares as projection onto the column space.
concepts.L2: Once regression is a projection, the normal equations stop being a formula to memorize and become geometrically obvious. Also: never solve least squares via the normal equations numerically — condition number squares. Use QR or SVD.
concepts.L3: The closest point of $\mathrm{col}(A)$ to b is the one whose residual is orthogonal to $\mathrm{col}(A): A^{T}(b - Ax) = 0$, which is the normal equations $A^{T} A x = A^{T} b$. When A has full column rank, A^T A is invertible, $x = (A^{T} A)^{-1}A^{T} b$, and $Ax = Pb$ with $P = A(A^{T} A)^{-1}A^{T}$. $P^{2} = P$ and $P^{T} = P$ are what make it an orthogonal rather than oblique projection. Gram-Schmidt orthonormalises the columns one at a time by subtracting projections onto the previous ones, and recording the coefficients gives A = QR; then $A^{T} A x = A^{T} b$ becomes $R^{T} Q^{T} Q R x = R^{T} Q^{T} b$, i.e. $Rx = Q^{T} b$ — one triangular solve, no squaring of the condition number.

concepts.L1: The condition number measures how much a relative perturbation of the input can be amplified in the output. It is the ratio of largest to smallest singular value, it is at least 1, and it equals 1 only for scaled orthogonal matrices.
concepts.L2: It is a property of the problem, not of your algorithm: no method recovers information that conditioning destroyed. A stable algorithm on an ill-conditioned problem still returns an inaccurate answer — the exact answer to a nearby problem. Confusing conditioning with stability is the standard misreading.
concepts.L3: From $Ax = b$ and $A(x + dx) = b + db, dx = A^{-1}db$, so $\|dx\| \leq \|A^{-1}\| \|db\|$; with $\|b\| \leq \|A\| \|x\|$ this gives $\|dx\|/\|x\| \leq \mathrm{cond}(A) \|db\|/\|b\|$, and in the 2-norm $\mathrm{cond}(A) = \sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}$. At unit roundoff 1e-16 the achievable accuracy is about $\mathrm{cond}(A) \cdot 1e-16$ whatever the algorithm. That is conditioning; backward stability is the separate question of whether your answer is exact for a nearby problem. Squaring is the trap: $\mathrm{cond}(A^{T} A) = \mathrm{cond}(A)^{2}$, so least squares goes through QR or SVD and never the normal equations, and a variance is never $\mathbb{E}[x^{2}] - \mathbb{E}[x]^{2}$.

L4.explanation: Verified: np.linalg.cond = 40002.000075. Nearly-parallel columns are the standard source of large condition numbers, and it is what collinear features do to a design matrix.
