L4.explanation: Verified in numpy with diagonal examples. Squaring the singular values squares the ratio — the whole reason least squares avoids the normal equations.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your solver is backward stable and $\mathrm{{ cond }}(A)$ = {k}. A colleague says switching to a better algorithm will fix the inaccurate answer. Respond.
L4.answer: It will not. Conditioning is a property of the problem: the exact solution itself is hypersensitive to the input data. A backward-stable algorithm already delivers the exact answer to a problem within rounding of yours. The fix is to change the problem — regularise, rescale, drop collinear features, or use higher precision.
L4.explanation: Stability bounds the extra error the algorithm adds; conditioning bounds the error inherent in the data. Only the second is fixed by reformulation.

concepts.t: Least squares and the normal equations

L0.body:
$\min_{x} \|Ax - b\|_{2}^{2}$.  Normal equations: $A^{T} A x = A^{T} b$.
Stable route: A = QR -> $R x = Q^{T} b$.  Rank-deficient route: $x = A^{+} b (SVD)$.
np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)   # uses SVD, handles rank deficiency
L0.cloze: Least squares solves {{c1::$A^{T} A x = A^{T} b$}}; $\mathrm{cond}(A^{T} A)$ = {{c2::$\mathrm{cond}(A)^{2}$}}, so prefer {{c3::QR or SVD}}.

concepts.L1: Least squares finds the x minimising $\|Ax - b\|^{2}$ when the system is overdetermined and has no exact solution. The minimiser satisfies the normal equations, and it is unique exactly when A has full column rank; otherwise a whole affine set of minimisers exists.
concepts.L2: The number that matters is $\mathrm{cond}(A^{T} A) = \mathrm{cond}(A)^{2}$. At condition number 1e8 — routine for correlated features — the normal equations lose all sixteen digits of double precision while QR loses eight. That is why lstsq uses SVD, and why hand-rolled inv(X.T@X)@X.T@y quietly produces garbage.
concepts.L3: Let $f(x) = \|Ax - b\|^{2} = x^{T} A^{T} A x - 2 b^{T} A x + b^{T} b$. Its gradient is $2A^{T} A x - 2A^{T} b$; setting it to zero gives the normal equations. The Hessian $2A^{T} A$ is PSD, so every stationary point is a global minimum — least squares is convex — and uniqueness needs $A^{T} A$ positive definite, i.e. full column rank. Conditioning: the singular values of $A^{T} A$ are the squares of A's, so $\mathrm{cond}_{2}(A^{T} A) = \mathrm{cond}_{2}(A)^{2}$, and forming $A^{T} A$ destroys information before the solve begins. QR gives $Rx = Q^{T} b$ with $\mathrm{cond}(R) = \mathrm{cond}(A)$. Ridge $(A^{T} A + \lambda I)$ fixes both uniqueness and conditioning at the price of bias.

L4.prompt_tpl: A = diag({s1}, {s2}). Compute $\mathrm{{ cond }}(A)$ and $\mathrm{{ cond }}(A^{{ T }} A)$. Answer with cond(A).
L4.answer: $\mathrm{cond}(A) = 3; \mathrm{cond}(A^{T} A) = 9$
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: $\mathrm{cond}(\mathrm{diag}(3,1)) = 3.0, \mathrm{cond}(\mathrm{diag}(9,1)) = 9.0$. Squaring, exactly as predicted.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your design matrix has estimated condition number {k}. In float64, which solver do you use and how many digits do you expect to keep?
L4.answer: For 1e8: QR or SVD (np.linalg.lstsq). Expect to lose about 8 digits of 16, keeping ~8. Normal equations would face cond 1e16 and keep essentially nothing.
L4.explanation: Rule of thumb: you lose about $\log_{10}(\mathrm{cond})$ digits. The normal equations double that loss because they square the condition number before solving.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that the least squares objective is convex and that any stationary point is a global minimum.
L4.answer: Hessian = $2A^{T} A$, and $x^{T} A^{T} A x = \|Ax\|^{2} \geq 0$, so the Hessian is PSD everywhere, so f is convex; for convex $f, \nabla f = 0$ implies a global minimum.
L4.explanation: This is why linear regression has no local-minimum problem at all, in contrast with every nonlinear model.

L0.body:
$P = [b_{1} b_{2} \dots b_{n}]$ (new basis vectors as columns) maps new coords -> old coords.
Same map in the new basis: $B = P^{-1} A P$.  A and B are similar.
Invariant under similarity: trace, det, rank, eigenvalues, characteristic polynomial.
L0.cloze: B = {{c1::$P^{-1} A P$}}; similar matrices share {{c2::eigenvalues}}, trace and determinant, but not {{c3::individual entries}}.

concepts.L1: Similar matrices are the same linear map written in different bases. The conversion is $P^{-1}AP$, where P's columns are the new basis expressed in the old one. Everything intrinsic to the map survives the change; everything else was a coordinate artefact.
concepts.L2: Read $P^{-1}AP$ right to left as a sentence: convert to the old basis, act, convert back. Getting P versus $P^{-1}$ backwards is the standard error and produces a matrix that is still similar to A, so the invariants still check out and the bug survives your sanity test. Verify on a specific vector instead.
concepts.L3: If $x_{\mathrm{new}}$ are coordinates in the new basis then $x_{\mathrm{old}} = P x_{\mathrm{new}}$. Applying the map in old coordinates gives $A P x_{\mathrm{new}}$, and converting back to new coordinates multiplies by $P^{-1}: B = P^{-1}AP$. Similarity is an equivalence relation. Invariants: $\mathrm{trace}(P^{-1}AP) = \mathrm{trace}(APP^{-1}) = \mathrm{trace}(A)$ by cyclicity; $\det (P^{-1}AP) = \det (P)^{-1}\det (A)\det (P) = \det (A)$; and if $Av = \lambda v$ then $B(P^{-1}v) = P^{-1}Av = \lambda (P^{-1}v)$, so eigenvalues match with eigenvectors carried across by $P^{-1}$. Diagonalization is the special case where the new basis is a basis of eigenvectors.

L4.prompt_tpl: $A = [[3,1],[0,2]], P = [[1,1],[0,1]]$. Compute $P^{{-1}}AP$ and check trace, determinant and eigenvalues.
L4.answer: $P^{-1}AP = [[3,2],[0,2]]; \mathrm{trace} 5, \det 6$, eigenvalues {3,2} — identical to A.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy. The (1,2) entry changed from 1 to 2; every invariant did not. Trace, determinant and spectrum are properties of the map; individual entries are properties of the basis you happened to write it in.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are told a matrix is similar to diag({d1},{d2},{d3}). What do you immediately know about it?
L4.answer: Eigenvalues 2, 3, 5; trace 10; determinant 30; rank 3; invertible; diagonalizable. It is the map that scales three independent directions by those factors.
L4.explanation: Verified arithmetic: $2+3+5 = 10, 2\cdot 3\cdot 5 = 30$. All the hard-looking questions about the matrix are answered by the diagonal form.

L4.prompt_tpl: Are A = [[1,{a}],[0,1]] and I similar?
L4.answer: No.
L4.explanation: They share trace 2, determinant 1 and eigenvalues {1,1}, so the invariants do not separate them — but $P^{-1}IP = I$ for every P, so the only matrix similar to I is I. A shear is not the identity. Matching invariants is necessary, never sufficient.

L0.body:
$Av = \lambda v, v \neq 0$.  $\det (A - \lambda I) = 0$ (characteristic polynomial).
For $2x_{2}: \lambda^{2} - \mathrm{trace}(A) \lambda + \det (A) = 0$.
$\sum \lambda_{i} = \mathrm{trace}(A); \prod \lambda_{i} = \det (A)$.
np.linalg.eig(A)  (general) ; np.linalg.eigh(A)  (symmetric — use this when you can)
L0.cloze: Av = {{c1::lambda v}}; eigenvalues solve {{c2::$\det (A - \lambda I) = 0$}}; for symmetric A the spectral theorem gives {{c3::real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors}}.

concepts.L1: Directions preserved up to scaling. Characteristic polynomial, algebraic vs geometric multiplicity, diagonalizability, the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices (real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors).
concepts.L2: Most matrices you meet in ML are symmetric or can be symmetrized — covariance matrices, Hessians, Gram matrices — which is why the spectral theorem does most of the work in practice.
concepts.L3: $Av = \lambda v$ with v nonzero says $(A - \lambda I)v = 0$ has a nontrivial solution, so A - lambda I is singular and $\det (A - \lambda I) = 0$ — a degree-n polynomial whose roots are the eigenvalues. Algebraic multiplicity is the root's multiplicity; geometric multiplicity is dim null(A - lambda I); geometric <= algebraic always, and A is diagonalizable exactly when they agree for every eigenvalue. The polynomial's coefficients give $\sum \lambda_{i} = \mathrm{trace}(A)$ and $\prod \lambda_{i} = \det (A)$, the cheapest sanity check on any hand computation. Defective matrices exist ([[1,1],[0,1]]), which is why the SVD, which never fails, is safer.

L4.prompt_tpl: Find the eigenvalues of $A = [[4,1],[2,3]]$ using trace and determinant.
L4.answer: $\lambda^{2} - 7 \lambda + 10 = 0$, so $\lambda = 5$ and 2.
L4.explanation: $\mathrm{trace} = 7, \det = 10$. Roots of $x^{2} - 7x + 10$ are 5 and $2; 5+2 = 7$ and $5\cdot 2 = 10$ check out. Verified with np.linalg.eigvals: [5., 2.].

L4.prompt_tpl: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the symmetric matrix [[{a},1],[1,{a}]].
L4.answer: $a=2$: eigenvalues 1 and 3, eigenvectors $[1,-1]/\sqrt{2}$ and $[1,1]/\sqrt{2}$. In general a-1 and $a+1$ with the same eigenvectors.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy for $a=2$ (eigvalsh gives [1,3]), $a=3 ([2,4]), a=4 ([3,5])$. The eigenvectors are orthogonal, as the spectral theorem requires.

L4.prompt_tpl: A = [[1,{a}],[0,1]]. Find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors and say whether it is diagonalizable.
L4.answer: Eigenvalue 1 with algebraic multiplicity 2, but $\mathrm{null}(A - I) = \mathrm{span}\{[1,0]\}$ is only 1-dimensional. Geometric multiplicity 1 < algebraic 2, so A is defective and not diagonalizable.
L4.explanation: A shear has exactly one invariant direction. This is the standard example of eigendecomposition failing to exist — and note that the SVD of this matrix exists regardless.

prereqs: Solving Ax = b: existence and uniqueness

L0.body:
$A = V \Lambda V^{-1}$ when A has n independent eigenvectors (columns of V).
$A^{k} = V \Lambda^{k} V^{-1}; e^{A} = V e^{\Lambda} V^{-1}$.
np.linalg.matrix_power(A, k)
L0.cloze: $A^{k}$ = {{c1::$V \Lambda^{k} V^{-1}$}}, so powers are governed by {{c2::the largest $|\lambda |$}}: it blows up if > 1 and vanishes if {{c3::< 1}}.

concepts.L1: If A has a full set of independent eigenvectors, $A = V \Lambda V^{-1}$ and every power becomes trivial: $A^{k} = V \Lambda^{k} V^{-1}$. Repeated application of a linear map is therefore governed entirely by the eigenvalues raised to the k-th power.
concepts.L2: This is the whole story of exploding and vanishing gradients in an RNN: the recurrence is a repeated matrix product, so the spectral radius decides whether signal grows or dies exponentially in sequence length. It also explains why the fix is spectral — orthogonal recurrent weights, gating — not a smaller step.
concepts.L3: If $Av_{i} = \lambda_{i} v_{i}$ for a basis $\{v_{i}\}$, stack them as columns of V; then AV = V Lambda, and independence makes V invertible, giving $A = V \Lambda V^{-1}$. Powers telescope: $A^{2} = V \Lambda V^{-1} V \Lambda V^{-1} = V \Lambda^{2} V^{-1}$, and by induction $A^{k} = V \Lambda^{k} V^{-1}$. Since $\Lambda^{k} = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{i}^{k})$, the behaviour as k grows is dominated by the largest $|\lambda_{i}|: A^{k} x \approx \lambda_{\max}^{k}$. Any analytic function of A is defined the same way, which is how matrix exponentials solve linear ODEs. Non-diagonalizable matrices need the Jordan form, where powers pick up polynomial-in-k factors.

L4.prompt_tpl: $A = [[2,1],[0,3]]$. Compute A^{k} using the eigenvalues.
L4.answer: Eigenvalues 2 and $3; A^{5} = [[32, 211],[0, 243]]$ (note 2^5 = 32, 3^5 = 243 on the diagonal).
L4.explanation: Verified with np.linalg.matrix_power: [[32,211],[0,243]]. The diagonal entries are exactly the eigenvalues to the fifth power, as triangularity requires.

L4.prompt_tpl: A recurrent weight matrix has spectral radius {r}. What happens to the hidden state norm over {T} timesteps, roughly? Answer with the growth factor over T steps.
L4.explanation: Verified: $0.9^{100} = 2.6561e-5; 1.1^{100} = 13780.6$. A 20% change in spectral radius produces nine orders of magnitude difference over 100 steps.

L4.prompt_tpl: $A = [[1,1],[1,0]]$ (the Fibonacci matrix). Compute A^{k} and identify the entries.
L4.answer: $A^{10} = [[89, 55],[55, 34]]$ — consecutive Fibonacci numbers $F(11), F(10), F(10), F(9)$.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy. The eigenvalues are the golden ratio and its conjugate, which is where Binet's closed form comes from — a clean demonstration that $A^{k} = V \Lambda^{k} V^{-1}$ is a closed form for a recurrence.

L0.body:
A symmetric $(A = A^{T}) \Rightarrow A = Q \Lambda Q^{T}$ with Q orthogonal and Lambda real diagonal.
Eigenvalues real; eigenvectors of distinct eigenvalues orthogonal.
$A = \sum_{i} \lambda_{i} q_{i} q_{i}^{T}$   (spectral decomposition into rank-1 projectors)
np.linalg.eigh(A)   # always for symmetric: faster and guarantees real output
L0.cloze: Symmetric matrices satisfy A = {{c1::$Q \Lambda Q^{T}$}} with Q {{c2::orthogonal}} and all eigenvalues {{c3::real}}.

concepts.L1: Every real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable: real eigenvalues, an orthonormal eigenbasis, $A = Q \Lambda Q^{T}$. Equivalently A is a weighted sum of orthogonal rank-1 projectors, so it acts by independent scaling along perpendicular axes.
concepts.L2: Use np.linalg.eigh, not eig, for symmetric matrices: eig can return complex values with tiny imaginary parts from rounding, and downstream code then either crashes or silently casts. Since covariances, Gram matrices and Hessians are all symmetric, eigh is what you should reach for by default.
concepts.L3: Real eigenvalues: if $Av = \lambda v$ with v possibly complex, then $v^{*} A v = \lambda \|v\|^{2}$; taking conjugate transposes and using $A = A^{T}$ real gives $v^{*} A v = \mathrm{conj}(\lambda)\|v\|^{2}$, so $\lambda = \mathrm{conj}(\lambda)$ is real. Orthogonality: if $Av = a v$ and $Aw = b w$ with $a \neq b$ then $a v^{T} w = (Av)^{T} w = v^{T} A w = b v^{T} w$, so $(a - b) v^{T} w = 0$ and $v^{T} w = 0$. Repeated eigenvalues still admit an orthonormal eigenbasis, by Gram-Schmidt within each eigenspace. Writing Q's columns as $q_{i}$ gives $A = \sum \lambda_{i} q_{i} q_{i}^{T}$, an orthogonal decomposition of the map into scalings along perpendicular directions.

L4.prompt_tpl: Diagonalize [[{a},1],[1,{a}]] orthogonally: give Lambda and Q.
L4.explanation: Verified with np.linalg.eigh: eigenvalues [1,3], orthonormal eigenvectors $[1,-1]/\sqrt{2}$ and $[1,1]/\sqrt{2}$. For $a=3$ the eigenvalues are [2,4] with the same eigenvectors.

L4.prompt_tpl: Prove that eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
L4.answer: $a v^{T} w = (Av)^{T} w = v^{T} A^{T} w = v^{T} A w = b v^{T} w$, so $(a-b)v^{T} w = 0$; since $a \neq b, v^{T} w = 0$.
L4.explanation: The only property used is $A = A^{T}$. It is a three-line proof and worth being able to reproduce cold, since it is the heart of PCA's orthogonal components.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have a {n}x{n} covariance matrix and need its eigendecomposition. eig or eigh, and why?
options: Either — they agree to machine precision
L4.answer: eigh.
L4.explanation: Covariance matrices are symmetric PSD. eigh exploits symmetry (roughly 2x faster, and it only reads one triangle), returns real values sorted ascending, and cannot produce spurious imaginary parts from rounding.

L0.body:
$q(x) = x^{T} A x = \sum_{ij} A_{ij} x_{i} x_{j}$.  WLOG A symmetric (replace A by $(A+A^{T})/2$).
In the eigenbasis: $q(x) = \sum_{i} \lambda_{i} y_{i}^{2}$ where $y = Q^{T} x$.
Level sets $\{q(x) = c\}$ are ellipses (all $\lambda > 0$), hyperbolas (mixed signs), or degenerate.
L0.cloze: $x^{T} A x$ depends only on {{c1::the symmetric part}} of A; in the eigenbasis it becomes {{c2::sum lambda_i y_i^2}}, so the signs of the {{c3::eigenvalues}} decide the shape.

concepts.L1: A quadratic form is $x^{T} A x$, the scalar output of a matrix sandwiched by a vector. Only A's symmetric part contributes. Rotating to the eigenbasis removes all cross terms and turns it into a weighted sum of squares whose coefficients are the eigenvalues.
concepts.L2: Any quadratic form has infinitely many matrices representing it, and exactly one symmetric one — which is why derivations that quietly assume symmetry give $\nabla (x^{T} A x) = 2Ax$ when the general answer is $(A + A^{T})x$. Getting this wrong is invisible on symmetric test cases and wrong everywhere else.
concepts.L3: Since $x^{T} A x$ is a scalar it equals its own transpose $x^{T} A^{T} x$, so $x^{T} A x = x^{T} ((A + A^{T})/2) x$: only the symmetric part survives. Apply the spectral theorem, $A = Q \Lambda Q^{T}$, and substitute $y = Q^{T} x$ (orthogonal, so lengths are unchanged): $q(x) = y^{T} \Lambda y = \sum_{i} \lambda_{i} y_{i}^{2}$. The cross terms are gone; the level set $q = 1$ is an ellipsoid with semi-axis lengths $1/\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$ along the eigenvectors when all $\lambda_{i} > 0$, a hyperboloid when signs are mixed, and unbounded in the directions of zero eigenvalues. This is the picture underneath 'the loss surface is an elongated valley' — the elongation is the eigenvalue ratio.

L4.explanation: $2(1) + 2(1)(2) + 3(4) = 2 + 4 + 12 = 18$. Verified in numpy: x @ A @ $x = 18$. Only the symmetric part of A contributes, so replacing A by $(A + A^{T})/2$ leaves every value of the form unchanged.

L4.prompt_tpl: What shape is the level set $x^{{ T }} A x = 1$ for A = [[1,{b}],[{b},1]]?
L4.answer: A hyperbola: the eigenvalues are 3 and -1, so signs are mixed.
L4.explanation: Verified: eigvalsh$([[1,2],[2,1]]) = [-1, 3]$. Mixed signs give a saddle-shaped form and hyperbolic level sets. With $b = 0.5$ the eigenvalues would be 0.5 and 1.5 and the level set would be an ellipse.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that $x^{{ T }} A x = x^{{ T }} ((A + A^{{ T }})/2) x$ for every x, and give a concrete A where 2Ax is not the gradient.
L4.answer: $x^{T} A x$ is a 1x1 matrix, hence equal to its transpose $x^{T} A^{T} x$; averaging the two gives the claim. For $A = [[1,2],[3,4]]$ and $x = [1,2]: 2Ax = [10,22]$ but $\nabla = (A+A^{T})x = [12,21]$.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy. The two agree only when A is symmetric, which is exactly why every matrix-calculus table states the general form.

L0.body:
A symmetric is PD iff $x^{T} A x > 0$ for all $x \neq 0$.
Equivalent: all $\lambda_{i} > 0; A = LL^{T}$ exists (Cholesky);  all leading principal minors > $0; A = B^{T} B$ with B full column rank.
np.linalg.cholesky(A)   # raises LinAlgError iff not PD — the cheapest test
L0.cloze: PD iff {{c1::$x^{T} A x > 0$}} for all nonzero x iff all eigenvalues {{c2::positive}} iff a {{c3::Cholesky}} factorization exists.

concepts.L1: xᵀAx > 0 for all nonzero x. Equivalent to all eigenvalues positive, to a Cholesky factorization existing, to all leading principal minors positive.
concepts.L2: This is the condition that makes a quadratic form have a unique minimum, which is why it's everywhere in optimization. A positive-definite Hessian means a local minimum; indefinite means a saddle — and saddles, not minima, are the dominant critical point in high dimensions.
concepts.L3: In the eigenbasis $x^{T} A x = \sum \lambda_{i} y_{i}^{2}$, positive for all nonzero y exactly when every $\lambda_{i} > 0$. Cholesky: with all $\lambda_{i} > 0, A = Q \Lambda Q^{T} = (Q \Lambda^{1/2})(Q \Lambda^{1/2})^{T}$; the triangular version $A = LL^{T}$ comes from elimination without pivoting at $(1/3)n^{3}$ — half of LU, since symmetry halves the work — and its success or failure is itself the PD test. Minors: Sylvester's criterion. Why saddles dominate: an extremum needs all n eigenvalues to share a sign, which is exponentially unlikely as n grows, so almost every critical point in a high-dimensional loss surface is a saddle.

L4.prompt_tpl: Is [[{a},-1],[-1,{a}]] positive definite? Give the eigenvalues and the Cholesky factor if it exists.
L4.answer: $a=2$: eigenvalues 1 and 3, both positive, so yes. Cholesky $L = [[1.41421356, 0],[-0.70710678, 1.22474487]]$.
L4.explanation: Verified: eigvalsh$([[2,-1],[-1,2]]) = [1,3]$; np.linalg.cholesky succeeds. Leading minors 2 > 0 and det 3 > 0 agree.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compute the Cholesky factor of [[4,2],[2,5]].
L4.explanation: Verified with np.linalg.cholesky: [[2,0],[1,2]]. $L L^{T} = [[4,2],[2,4+1]] = [[4,2],[2,5]]$. Cholesky succeeding is itself the cheapest positive-definiteness test: half the cost of an eigendecomposition and with no iteration.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Hessian at a critical point has eigenvalues {evs}. Classify the point and say what gradient descent does there.
L4.answer: {2,8}: PD, a strict local minimum. {-1,5}: indefinite, a saddle — descent escapes along the negative-curvature direction but slowly, since the gradient is small nearby. {0,3}: PSD but singular, inconclusive at second order.
L4.explanation: In high dimensions the indefinite case dominates: needing all n eigenvalues to share a sign is exponentially unlikely, which is the modern answer to 'why doesn't non-convexity kill deep learning'.

L0.body:
$A = U \Sigma V^{T}$ for ANY m x n matrix. U (m x m) and V (n x n) orthogonal; Sigma diagonal, $\sigma_{1} \geq \dots \geq \sigma_{r} > 0$.
$\sigma_{i} = \sqrt{\lambda_{i}(A^{T} A)}$;  columns of V are eigenvectors of $A^{T} A; u_{i} = A v_{i} / \sigma_{i}$.
$A = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_{i} u_{i} v_{i}^{T}$
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)
L0.cloze: A = {{c1::$U \Sigma V^{T}$}} exists for {{c2::every}} matrix; the singular values are {{c3::sqrt of the eigenvalues of $A^{T} A$}}.

concepts.L1: A = UΣVᵀ for any matrix. Singular values are the square roots of eigenvalues of AᵀA. Eckart-Young: truncating to the top k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation in Frobenius and spectral norm.
concepts.L2: SVD is the most important decomposition in machine learning. Low-rank approximation via Eckart-Young is the direct mathematical justification for LoRA, for PCA, for embedding compression, and for the low-rank structure people find in trained weights.
concepts.L3: $A^{T} A$ is symmetric PSD, so the spectral theorem gives $A^{T} A = V \Lambda V^{T}$ with $\lambda_{i} \geq 0$. Set $\sigma_{i} = \sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$ and $u_{i} = A v_{i}/\sigma_{i}$ for $\sigma_{i} > 0$. These are orthonormal: $u_{i}^{T} u_{j} = v_{i}^{T} A^{T} A v_{j}/(\sigma_{i} \sigma_{j}) = \delta_{ij}$. Then $A v_{i} = \sigma_{i} u_{i}$, i.e. AV = U Sigma, i.e. $A = U \Sigma V^{T}$. Geometrically every linear map is a rotation/reflection, an axis-aligned scaling, and another rotation/reflection — nothing more. Unlike eigendecomposition it always exists, needs no squareness, and is stable, which is why rank, pseudoinverse, least squares and cond are all built on it.

L4.prompt_tpl: $A = [[4,0],[3,-5]]$. Compute the singular values, $\|A\|_{{2}}, \|A\|_{{ F }}$ and $\mathrm{{ cond }}_{{2}}(A)$.
Show that the singular values of A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^{{ T }} A$.
L4.answer: $A^{T} A = (U \Sigma V^{T})^{T} (U \Sigma V^{T}) = V \Sigma^{T} U^{T} U \Sigma V^{T} = V \Sigma^{2} V^{T}$, which is an eigendecomposition with eigenvalues $\sigma_{i}^{2}$.
L4.explanation: Symmetrically $A A^{T} = U \Sigma^{2} U^{T}$, so U holds the eigenvectors of $A A^{T}$. This is also why forming $A^{T} A$ to get singular values squares the condition number and is numerically inferior to a direct SVD.

L4.prompt_tpl: A is {m}x{n} of rank {r}. What are the shapes of U, Sigma, V in the thin SVD, and how many singular values are nonzero?
L4.answer: Thin SVD (full_matrices=False): U is 1000x50, Sigma is 50x50, V is 50x50. Exactly 30 nonzero singular values.
L4.explanation: The number of nonzero singular values is the rank, which is the numerically meaningful definition of rank.

L0.body:
$A_{k} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_{i} u_{i} v_{i}^{T}$  (truncated SVD).
$\min_{\mathrm{rank}(B) \leq k} \|A - B\|_{F} = \sqrt{\sum_{i>k} \sigma_{i}^{2}}; \min \|A - B\|_{2} = \sigma_{k+1}$.
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False); $A_{k} = (U[:,:k] \cdot s[:k])$ @ Vt[:k]
L0.cloze: The best rank-k approximation is {{c1::the truncated SVD}}; the spectral-norm error is {{c2::$\sigma_{k+1}$}} and the Frobenius error is {{c3::$\sqrt{\sum_{i>k} \sigma_{i}^{2}}$}}.

concepts.L1: Truncating the SVD at k terms is provably the best rank-k approximation, in both Frobenius and spectral norm — no cleverer rank-k matrix exists. The error is read directly off the discarded singular values, so the spectrum tells you in advance how much compression costs.
concepts.L2: 'Optimal' means in those two norms, and it is about reconstructing the matrix, not preserving task performance. A truncation keeping 99% of Frobenius energy can still destroy the small-singular-value directions a classifier depends on, which is why naive SVD compression underperforms trained adapters.
concepts.L3: Spectral case: for any B of rank <= k, null(B) has dimension >= n - k, so it intersects the $(k+1)$-dimensional $\mathrm{span}\{v_{1}\dots v_{k+1}\}$ nontrivially. Take a unit x in that intersection: $(A - B)x = Ax$, and since x lies in the top$-(k+1)$ right singular subspace, $\|Ax\| \geq \sigma_{k+1}$. Hence $\|A - B\|_{2} \geq \sigma_{k+1}$, and the truncation achieves it. The Frobenius case follows from a similar argument plus unitary invariance of the norm. Practical consequence: plot the singular values; a sharp elbow means cheap compression, a slow decay means none is available. Storage falls from mn to $k(m + n + 1)$, a win once $k < m_{n}/(m+n)$.

L4.prompt_tpl: $A = [[4,0],[3,-5]]$ has singular values (6.32455532, 3.16227766). What is the error of the best rank-1 approximation in spectral and Frobenius norm?
L4.answer: Both equal $\sigma_{2} = 3.16227766 (= \sqrt{10})$.
L4.explanation: Verified: only one discarded singular value, so the Frobenius error $\sqrt{\sum_{i>1} \sigma_{i}^{2}} = \sigma_{2}$ coincides with the spectral error. They differ whenever more than one term is dropped.

L4.prompt_tpl: A weight matrix is {m}x{n}. How much storage does a rank-{k} factorization save, as a ratio? Answer with the storage reduction ratio.
L4.explanation: Verified arithmetic: $16777216/131072 = 128.0; 16777216/524288 = 32.0$. This is exactly the LoRA parameter budget calculation.

L4.prompt_tpl: The singular values of a layer decay as {decay}. Is low-rank compression a good idea?
L4.answer: $1/i^{2}$: yes — energy sum sigma_i^2 ~ sum 1/i^4 converges fast, so a small k captures nearly everything. $1/\sqrt{i}$: no — sum sigma_i^2 ~ sum 1/i diverges logarithmically, energy is spread across all directions and truncation is expensive.
L4.explanation: The decision is read off the spectrum, not guessed. Always plot the singular values before proposing a low-rank scheme.

concepts.t: PCA as SVD of centered data

L0.body:
X (n samples x d features).  $Xc = X - X$.mean(0).
Covariance $C = Xc^{T} Xc / (n-1)$.  Principal components = eigenvectors of C = right singular vectors of Xc.
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
explained_variance = $s^{2} / (n - 1)$;  scores = Xc @ Vt[:k].T
L0.cloze: PCA = SVD of the {{c1::centered}} data; component variances are {{c2::$s^{2}/(n-1)$}}; forgetting to center gives {{c3::the direction of the mean}} as the first component.

concepts.L1: PCA finds the orthogonal directions of maximum variance in centered data. They are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, equivalently the right singular vectors of the centered data matrix, and the variance along each is $\sigma_{i}^{2}/(n-1)$.
concepts.L2: Compute it from the SVD of Xc, never from an eigendecomposition of $Xc^{T} Xc$: forming the covariance squares the condition number and can lose half your digits. And centering is not optional — skip it and the first component points at the mean, which is usually the least interesting direction in the data.
concepts.L3: Maximise variance of the projection onto a unit $w: \mathrm{Var} = w^{T} C w$ subject to $\|w\| = 1$. The Lagrangian gives $Cw = \lambda w$, so the maximiser is the top eigenvector of C and the maximised variance is the top eigenvalue. Subsequent components maximise the same thing subject to orthogonality, yielding the remaining eigenvectors in order. Substituting the SVD $Xc = U \Sigma V^{T}$ gives $C = V \Sigma^{2} V^{T}/(n-1)$, so V holds the eigenvectors and $\lambda_{i} = \sigma_{i}^{2}/(n-1)$ — the SVD route needs no covariance matrix at all. Reconstruction from the top k components is exactly the Eckart-Young truncation, so PCA is the minimum-reconstruction-error linear encoder.

L4.prompt_tpl: Data rows: (2,0), (0,1), (-2,0), (0,-1). Find the mean, the covariance matrix, and the first principal component with its variance.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: the data is already centered; $Xc^{T} Xc/(n-1) = \mathrm{diag}(8/3, 2/3)$. The x-direction carries 80% of the variance.

L4.prompt_tpl: Data rows (1,2), (2,4), (3,6), (4,8). How many nonzero singular values does the centered matrix have, and what fraction of variance does PC1 explain? Answer with the number of nonzero singular values.
L4.answer: One nonzero singular value (5.0); PC1 = [0.4472136, 0.8944272] explains 100% of the variance.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: singular values [5.0, 0.0]. The points are perfectly collinear, so the centered data is rank 1 and one component captures everything.

L4.prompt_tpl: You run PCA on data with mean [{m1}, {m2}] but forget to center. What does PC1 come out as, and why?
L4.answer: Approximately the direction of the mean, [100,50] normalised, because uncentered $X^{T} X$ is dominated by n * mean mean^T when the mean is large relative to the spread.
L4.explanation: The uncentered second-moment matrix equals the covariance plus n * mean mean^T. With a large mean that rank-1 term swamps everything and PC1 just recovers the offset.

L0.body:
$A = U \Sigma V^{T} \Rightarrow A^{+} = V \Sigma^{+} U^{T}$, where $\Sigma^{+}$ inverts the nonzero singular values and transposes.
Full column $\mathrm{rank}: A^{+} = (A^{T} A)^{-1} A^{T}$ (least squares).  Full $\mathrm{row} \mathrm{rank}: A^{+} = A^{T} (A A^{T})^{-1}$ (minimum norm).
$x = A^{+} b$ is the least-squares solution of smallest $\|x\|$.
np.linalg.pinv(A) ; np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)
L0.cloze: $A^{+}$ = {{c1::$V \Sigma^{+} U^{T}$}}; $x = A^{+} b$ minimises {{c2::$\|Ax - b\|$}} and, among all minimisers, has smallest {{c3::$\|x\|$}}.

concepts.L1: The pseudoinverse inverts a matrix on the parts where inversion makes sense: it maps the column space back to the row space and sends the left null space to zero. $x = A^{+}b$ is always defined and always gives the minimum-norm least-squares solution.
concepts.L2: It answers both failure modes at once — no solution (minimise the residual) and infinitely many (take the shortest). The quiet danger is rcond: singular values below the cutoff are treated as zero, so the answer depends on a tolerance, and an ill-conditioned problem can flip when you change it.
concepts.L3: Write $A = U \Sigma V^{T}$ with rank r. Define $A^{+} = V \Sigma^{+} U^{T}$ where $\Sigma^{+}$ has $1/\sigma_{i}$ for $i \leq r$ and zeros elsewhere. Then $A A^{+}$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\mathrm{col}(A)$ and $A^{+} A$ is the projector onto $\mathrm{row}(A)$, so $A A^{+} b$ is the closest reachable point to b — the least-squares property. Any other minimiser differs by a null-space vector n, and since $A^{+} b$ lies in $\mathrm{row}(A)$ which is orthogonal to $\mathrm{null}(A)$, Pythagoras gives $\|A^{+} b + n\|^{2} = \|A^{+} b\|^{2} + \|n\|^{2} > \|A^{+} b\|^{2}$ for n nonzero: the minimum-norm property. The four Moore-Penrose conditions characterise it uniquely.

L4.prompt_tpl: $A = [[1, 1]]$ and b = [{b}]. Find all solutions of $Ax = b$ and the minimum-norm one.
L4.answer: All: $x = [t, 4 - t]$. Minimum norm: $x = [2, 2] = A^{+} b$.
L4.explanation: Verified: np.linalg.pinv([[1,1]]) @ $[4] = [2,2]$. The solution set is a line; the closest point of that line to the origin is where the line meets $\mathrm{row}(A) = \mathrm{span}\{[1,1]\}$.
Verified with np.linalg.pinv. The result lies in $\mathrm{row}(A) = \mathrm{span}\{[1,2,3]\}$, as the minimum-norm property requires: it is $[1,2,3]/14$.

L4.prompt_tpl: np.linalg.lstsq with rcond={r1} and rcond={r2} give very different answers for the same system. Explain.
L4.answer: rcond sets the threshold below which singular values are treated as zero. Raising it discards near-null directions, which regularises the solution (smaller norm, more stable) but changes it. The system is ill-conditioned, so the answer is genuinely tolerance-dependent.
L4.explanation: This is a signal, not a nuisance: a solution that swings with rcond means the data does not determine those directions. The honest fixes are ridge regularisation or dropping features, not picking the rcond you like.

prereqs: Least squares and the normal equations

L0.body:
Numerator (Jacobian) layout: for $f: \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, df/dx$ is $m x n, (df/dx)_{ij} = df_{i}/dx_{j}$.
Gradient of a scalar: $\nabla f = (df/dx)^{T}$, a column in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.
Chain rule: $d(f o g)/dx = (df/dg)(dg/dx)$  — Jacobians multiply, right to left.
Hessian: $H_{ij} = d^{2} f / dx_{i} dx_{j}$, symmetric for $C^{2}$ functions.
L0.cloze: Jacobians {{c1::multiply}} under the chain rule; $\nabla (x^{T} A x)$ = {{c2::$(A + A^{T})x$}}; $d(\mathrm{tr}(AX))/dX$ = {{c3::$A^{T}$}}.

concepts.L1: Gradients, Jacobians, Hessians. Layout conventions (numerator vs denominator). The chain rule in matrix form. Derivatives of traces, determinants, and quadratic forms.
concepts.L2: This is the specific competence that makes backpropagation derivable rather than memorized. Most people who 'know' backprop know the algorithm and cannot derive the gradient of a matrix product, which falls apart the moment they need a custom layer.
concepts.L3: The reliable method is differentials, which sidesteps layout entirely. Write df as a linear function of dX, then read off the derivative. For $f = x^{T} A x: df = dx^{T} A x + x^{T} A dx = x^{T}(A^{T} + A)dx$, so $\nabla f = (A + A^{T})x$. For $f = \mathrm{tr}(A^{T} X): df = \mathrm{tr}(A^{T} dX)$, so $df/dX = A$. For $f = \log \det X: d(\log \det X) = \mathrm{tr}(X^{-1} dX)$, so the derivative is $X^{-T}$. For Y = AXB: $dY = A dX B$, and pairing with an upstream gradient G via $\langle G, dY\rangle = \mathrm{tr}(G^{T} A dX B) = \mathrm{tr}(B G^{T} A dX)$ gives $dL/dX = A^{T} G B^{T}$. The differential is convention-free, which is why it is the safe route.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive $dL/dW$ for Y = XW with X of shape {n}x{d} and W of shape {d}x{k}, given $G = dL/dY$.
L4.answer: $dL/dW = X^{T} G$ (shape d x k = 768x256); $dL/dX = G W^{T}$ (shape $n x d = 32x_{768}$).
L4.explanation: From $dY = X dW, \langle G, dY\rangle = \mathrm{tr}(G^{T} X dW)$ so $dL/dW = X^{T} G$. Shape-checking alone determines the answer here: only $X^{T} G$ has shape 768x256. This is the linear layer backward pass.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compute $\nabla_{{ x }} (x^{{ T }} A x)$ for A = [[{a},{b}],[{c},{d}]] at $x = [1,2]$, with A not symmetric.
L4.explanation: $A + A^{T} = [[2,5],[5,8]]$; times [1,2] gives $[2+10, 5+16] = [12,21]$. Verified in numpy. Note $2Ax = [10,22]$ is the wrong answer here.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using differentials, derive d(log det X)/dX.
L4.explanation: $d(\log \det X) = \mathrm{tr}(X^{-1} dX)$ via Jacobi's formula, so the derivative with respect to X is $X^{-T}$. This appears in every Gaussian log-likelihood and in normalizing-flow objectives.

concepts.t: Matrix calculus identities you must know cold

L0.body:
$
abla_{x} (a^{T} x) = a$.       $
abla_{x} (x^{T} A x) = (A + A^{T})x$  [= 2Ax if A symmetric].
$
abla_{x} \|Ax - b\|^{2} = 2A^{T}(Ax - b)$.    $
abla_{X} \mathrm{tr}(A^{T} X) = A$.
$
abla_{X} \log \det X = X^{-T}$.   $d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1} dX X^{-1}$.
tr(AB) = tr(BA);  tr(A) = sum of eigenvalues.  Y = AXB => $dL/dX = A^{T} (dL/dY) B^{T}$.

concepts.L1: A short list carries most of ML: gradient of a linear form, of a quadratic form, of a squared residual, of a trace, of a log-determinant, plus the cyclic property of trace and the derivative of an inverse. Everything else is these plus the chain rule.
concepts.L2: Learn to derive them with differentials rather than memorising a table, because the table entries differ between sources by transposes depending on layout convention, and a memorised entry from the wrong convention is a bug you cannot see. Derive, then check numerically on a random non-symmetric matrix.
concepts.L3: All follow from writing df as a linear functional of the perturbation. Linear: $d(a^{T} x) = a^{T} dx$, so the gradient is a. Residual: $d\|Ax-b\|^{2} = 2(Ax-b)^{T} A dx$, giving $2A^{T}(Ax-b)$ — set to zero and you have the normal equations. Inverse: differentiate $X X^{-1} = I$ to get $dX X^{-1} + X d(X^{-1}) = 0$, hence $d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1} dX X^{-1}$. Trace cyclicity: $\mathrm{tr}(AB) = \sum_{ij} A_{ij} B_{ji} = \mathrm{tr}(BA)$, which is what lets you rotate a product until dX sits on the right and the coefficient can be read off. The Frobenius inner product $\langle G, dY\rangle = \mathrm{tr}(G^{T} dY)$ is the pairing that converts every such expression into a gradient.

L4.explanation: $Ax = 0$, so $Ax - b = [-1,-1]; A^{T}[-1,-1] = [-1,-s]$; times 2 gives [-2,-2s]. Verified in numpy for $s=2: [-2,-4]$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive $d(X^{{-1}})$ from $X X^{{-1}} = I$.
L4.explanation: The scalar analogue is $d(1/x) = -dx/x^{2}$; the matrix version keeps the two factors on opposite sides because multiplication does not commute.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need $\mathrm{{ tr }}(A B)$ where A is {m}x{n} and B is {n}x{m} with $m >> n$. Which order do you form the product in, and what does it cost? Answer with the FLOP count of forming BA and taking its trace.
L4.answer: Form BA $(n x n = 8x_{8})$ and take its $\mathrm{trace}: 2\cdot 8\cdot 100000\cdot 8 = 1.28e7 \mathrm{FLOPs}$, versus AB (100000x100000) at 1.6e11 FLOPs and 80 GB of storage. Better still, tr(AB) = sum(A * B.T) elementwise, at $2m_{n} = 1.6e6 \mathrm{FLOPs}$.
L4.explanation: Verified arithmetic: $2\cdot n\cdot m\cdot n = 2\cdot 8\cdot 1e5\cdot 8 = 1.28e7; 2\cdot m\cdot n\cdot m = 2\cdot 1e5\cdot 8\cdot 1e5 = 1.6e11$. Trace cyclicity is not a curiosity — it is the difference between feasible and impossible.

L0.body:
Floating point: 1 + eps == 1 for eps < 2^-53 ~ 1.1e-16 (float64); ~6e-8 (float32); ~1e-3 (bfloat16).
Catastrophic cancellation: subtracting nearly equal numbers destroys significant digits.
Iterative: power iteration (top eigenpair), Lanczos (Krylov, symmetric), conjugate gradient (solve $Ax=b$ for SPD A in <= n steps, faster if the spectrum clusters).
np.linalg.cond, scipy.sparse.linalg.cg, scipy.sparse.linalg.eigsh
L0.cloze: cond amplifies {{c1::relative error}}; QR is stable where {{c2::the normal equations}} square the condition number; CG converges in about {{c3::$\sqrt{\kappa}$}} iterations.

concepts.L1: Condition number and error amplification. Why floating point makes mathematically equivalent formulations numerically different. Stability of QR vs normal equations. Iterative methods: power iteration, Lanczos, conjugate gradient.
concepts.L2: Almost entirely absent from ML curricula and it's why people ship models with silent numerical bugs. The condition number of your Gram matrix explains a lot of mysterious training instability.
concepts.L3: Floating point has fixed relative precision: each operation returns the exact result rounded, with relative error at most the unit roundoff. Errors compound benignly under multiplication and catastrophically under subtraction of near-equal quantities, where leading digits cancel and trailing garbage is promoted — which is why the quadratic formula, variance as $\mathbb{E}[x^{2}] - \mathbb{E}[x]^{2}$, and the normal equations each have stable and unstable forms of the same mathematics. Conjugate gradient minimises the A-norm error over a Krylov subspace, giving $((\sqrt{\kappa}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa}+1))^{k}$: the square root is the point, and it is the same one momentum exploits.

L4.prompt_tpl: In float32 $(\epsilon \approx 1.19e-7)$, what does (1.0 + {e}) - 1.0 evaluate to?
L4.explanation: Verified: np.float32(1.0) + np.float32(1e-8) rounds back to 1.0 because 1e-8 < eps/2 in float32, so the subtraction returns exactly 0. This is why accumulators are kept in float32 or float64 even in mixed-precision training.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compute the sample variance of {n} values all near {mu}. Which formula, $\mathbb{{ E }}[x^{{2}}] - \mathbb{{ E }}[x]^{{2}}$ or the two-pass sum of squared deviations?
L4.answer: Two-pass.
L4.explanation: $\mathbb{E}[x^{2}]$ and $\mathbb{E}[x]^{2}$ are both about 1e12 while their difference is small, so cancellation destroys most significant digits — the one-pass formula can even return a negative variance. The two-pass version (or Welford's online algorithm) subtracts the mean first and never forms large near-equal quantities.

L4.prompt_tpl: For an SPD system with $\mathrm{{ cond }}(A)$ = {k}, roughly how many CG iterations to reduce the error by 1e-6, and how does that compare to gradient descent? Answer with the number of CG iterations.
L4.answer: CG: rate $(\sqrt{1e4}-1)/(\sqrt{1e4}+1) = 99/101 = 0.980$; iterations ~ $\ln (1e-6)/\ln (0.980) \approx 691$. Gradient descent: rate $(1e4-1)/(1e4+1) = 0.9998$; iterations ~ 69,078. Roughly 100x fewer, the $\sqrt{\kappa}$ speedup.

prereqs: Least squares and the normal equations

L0.body:
$v \leftarrow A v / \|A v\|$;  repeat.  Converges to the top eigenvector at rate $|\lambda_{2}/\lambda_{1}|^{k}$.
Rayleigh quotient estimate: $\lambda \approx v^{T} A v / (v^{T} v)$.
for _ in range$(k): v = A$ @ v; v /= np.linalg.norm(v)
scipy.sparse.linalg.eigsh(A, k=1)   # Lanczos: much better in practice
L0.cloze: Power iteration converges at rate {{c1::$|\lambda_{2}/\lambda_{1}|^{k}$}}; it needs only {{c2::matrix-vector products}}, never the matrix itself.

concepts.L1: Repeatedly multiplying a vector by A and renormalising drives it toward the dominant eigenvector, because the largest eigenvalue's component grows fastest. It needs only the ability to compute Av — the matrix never has to be formed.
concepts.L2: Convergence is governed by the eigenvalue gap, not the matrix size: at $\lambda_{2}/\lambda_{1} = 0.99$ you need hundreds of iterations, and with a tied top eigenvalue it never converges. This is the mechanism behind PageRank, behind spectral normalization, and behind Hessian probes that only have matvecs.
concepts.L3: Expand $v_{0} = \sum c_{i} q_{i}$ in an eigenbasis. Then $A^{k} v_{0} = \sum c_{i} \lambda_{i}^{k} q_{i} = \lambda_{1}^{k} (c_{1} q_{1} + \sum_{i>1} c_{i} (\lambda_{i}/\lambda_{1})^{k} q_{i})$. Every ratio $|\lambda_{i}/\lambda_{1}| < 1$, so all non-dominant terms decay geometrically and the direction converges to $q_{1}$ at rate $|\lambda_{2}/\lambda_{1}|^{k}$. Normalising each step prevents overflow but not the direction. Failure modes: $c_{1} = 0$ (measure zero), $|\lambda_{2}| = |\lambda_{1}|$ (no convergence), and a real matrix with complex dominant pair (rotation, no fixed direction). The Rayleigh quotient converges twice as fast for symmetric matrices.

L4.prompt_tpl: $A = [[2,1],[1,2]], v_{{0}} = [1,0]$. Run {k} power iterations (unnormalised) and give the Rayleigh quotient.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy. Convergence rate $|\lambda_{2}/\lambda_{1}| = 1/3$, and the Rayleigh quotient error falls roughly as $(1/3)^{2k}$ — quadratically faster than the vector itself.

L4.prompt_tpl: $\lambda_{{1}}$ = {l1} and $\lambda_{{2}}$ = {l2}. How many iterations to reduce the eigenvector error by 1e-3?
L4.answer: About 687 iterations.
L4.explanation: Verified: $\ln (1e-3)/\ln (0.99) = 687.3$. A 1% spectral gap makes power iteration nearly useless on its own; Lanczos or a shift-and-invert strategy is the practical answer.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need the top singular value of a {n}x{n} weight matrix every training step, for spectral normalization. Why is power iteration the right tool?
L4.answer: A full SVD is $O(n^{3})$ per step, hopeless. Power iteration on $W^{T} W$ costs two matvecs, $O(n^{2})$, and the persistent vector is carried across steps so a single iteration per step suffices — the weights change slowly, so the estimate stays converged.
L4.explanation: Verified cost comparison: $4096^{3} = 6.87e10$ versus $2\cdot 4096^{2} = 3.36e7$, a factor of 2048. Amortising the iteration across training steps is the trick that makes it free.

L0.body:
Level 1: vector-vector (axpy, dot) — $O(n) \mathrm{FLOPs}$ on $O(n)$ data.
Level 2: matrix-vector (gemv) — $O(n^{2}) \mathrm{FLOPs}$ on $O(n^{2})$ data.
Level 3: matrix-matrix (gemm) — $O(n^{3}) \mathrm{FLOPs}$ on $O(n^{2})$ data.
Arithmetic intensity = FLOPs / bytes moved. Roofline: compute-bound iff AI > $peak_{\mathrm{FLOPs}} / peak$_bandwidth.
L0.cloze: Only {{c1::Level 3}} (gemm) has arithmetic intensity that grows with n; Levels 1 and 2 are {{c2::memory-bound}} at intensity ~{{c3::1}}.

concepts.L1: BLAS is tiered by arithmetic intensity: level 1 and 2 do $O(1)$ arithmetic per element touched and are limited by memory bandwidth, while level 3 does $O(n)$ arithmetic per element and is the only tier that can saturate a modern processor's compute units.
concepts.L2: This is why every efficient ML kernel is written to become a gemm, and why batching helps even when it does no less arithmetic. Batch size 1 turns your matmul into a matvec, drops arithmetic intensity to about 1, and leaves the accelerator idle waiting on memory. Same FLOPs, different wall clock.
concepts.L3: For an m x k by k x n gemm: 2mnk FLOPs against $(m_{k} + k_{n} + m_{n})$ elements moved, giving arithmetic intensity 2mnk/(bytes). For square n and fp16, that is $2n^{3}/(6n^{2}) = n/3$ — growing with n. For gemv, $2n^{2} \mathrm{FLOPs}$ against about $n^{2}$ elements, so intensity ~1 regardless of n. Modern accelerators have FLOP-to-bandwidth ratios in the hundreds (an A100 delivers roughly 312 TFLOP/s fp16 against $2 TB/s$, a ratio near 156), so anything with intensity below that is bandwidth-bound. This is the roofline model, and it explains the entire kernel-fusion agenda: fusing elementwise operations into a gemm removes memory round-trips, not arithmetic.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compute the arithmetic intensity of an {m}x{k} by {k}x{n} gemm in fp16 (2 bytes/element), counting the three matrices moved once each.
L4.answer: $\mathrm{FLOPs} = 2\cdot 8192\cdot 128\cdot 8192 = 1.7180e10$; bytes = $2\cdot (8192\cdot 8192 + 8192\cdot 128 + 8192\cdot 128) = 1.3841e8$; AI = 124.12 FLOPs/byte.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: $2\cdot 8192\cdot 128\cdot 8192 / (2\cdot (8192\cdot 8192 + 2\cdot 8192\cdot 128)) = 124.12$. This matches NVIDIA's own worked example, where it lands just below the V100 roofline and is therefore memory-limited.

L4.prompt_tpl: Same shapes but a square {n}x{n} by {n}x{n} gemm in fp16. Compute the arithmetic intensity.
L4.answer: $\mathrm{FLOPs} = 2\cdot 1024^{3} = 2.1475e9$; bytes = $2\cdot 3\cdot 1024^{2} = 6.2915e6$; AI = 341.33 FLOPs/byte.
L4.explanation: Verified: $2147483648/6291456 = 341.33 = n/3$ with $n = 1024$. Well above the ~156 ratio of an A100, so this shape is compute-bound — which is the regime you want.

L4.prompt_tpl: Inference at batch size 1 on a {n}x{n} weight matrix is 50x slower per token than at batch size {b}. Explain without reference to FLOPs.
L4.answer: Batch 1 is a gemv: arithmetic intensity ~1, so time is set by reading the weights from memory, not by arithmetic. Batching reuses each loaded weight across b rows, raising intensity toward the compute-bound regime; the weights are read once for the whole batch.
L4.explanation: Verified: gemv AI = $2\cdot 4096^{2}/(2\cdot (4096^{2} + 2\cdot 4096)) \approx 1.0$. Per-token FLOPs are identical in both cases — this is a bandwidth story, and it is why autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and why speculative decoding and batching exist.

concepts.t: Why matmul is the unit of ML compute

L0.body:
Dense layer forward: Y = XW  -> 2 * batch * $d_{\mathrm{in}} \cdot d_{\mathrm{out}} \mathrm{FLOPs}$.
Backward: $dL/dX = G W^{T}$ and $dL/dW = X^{T} G$ — two more matmuls of the same size.
So training $\mathrm{FLOPs} \approx 3x$ forward. Transformer rule of thumb: $C \approx 6 \cdot N \cdot D$ (params N, tokens D).
torch.matmul / F.linear -> cuBLAS gemm -> tensor cores
L0.cloze: Backprop through Y = XW needs {{c1::two}} more matmuls, so training costs about {{c2::3x}} the forward pass, giving C ~ {{c3::6ND}}.

concepts.L1: Almost every FLOP in training a transformer is inside a matmul: the forward pass is one per linear layer, and backprop adds two of the same shape. That is why total training compute is approximately 6 * parameters * tokens, and why hardware is designed around gemm rather than around neural networks.
concepts.L2: The corollary is architectural: an operation that cannot be expressed as a matmul is priced out, however elegant. Depthwise convolutions and many sparse schemes have excellent FLOP counts and poor wall-clock times for exactly this reason — the unit of cost is the well-shaped gemm, not the FLOP.
concepts.L3: For Y = XW with X of shape $(B, d_{\mathrm{in}})$ and W of shape $(d_{\mathrm{in}}, d_{\mathrm{out}})$, the forward pass costs $2\cdot B\cdot d_{\mathrm{in}}\cdot d_{\mathrm{out}} \mathrm{FLOPs}$ — one multiply and one add per term. Backward needs $dL/dW = X^{T} G$ and $dL/dX = G W^{T}$, each at the same cost again. Total $6\cdot B\cdot d_{\mathrm{in}}\cdot d_{\mathrm{out}}$, i.e. 6 FLOPs per parameter per token, which is exactly the $C = 6$ND scaling-law accounting. Hardware follows: tensor cores implement a fixed-size multiply-accumulate as one instruction, so peak throughput needs shapes that tile onto them — hence padding to multiples of 8, 16 or 128.

L4.prompt_tpl: A model has {N} parameters and is trained on {D} tokens. Estimate total training FLOPs, and the time on {gpus} A100s at 50% of 312 TFLOP/s. Answer with the total training FLOPs.
L4.answer: $C = 6 \cdot 7e9 \cdot 2e12 = 8.4e22 \mathrm{FLOPs}$. Throughput = $1024 \cdot 312e12 \cdot 0.5 = 1.597e17 \mathrm{FLOP}/s$. Time = $8.4e22/1.597e17 = 5.258e5 s \approx 6.09$ days.
L4.explanation: Verified: $6\cdot 7e9\cdot 2e12 = 8.4e22; 1024\cdot 1.56e14 = 1.5974e17$; ratio $525,841 s = 146.1 h = 6.09$ days. The 6ND rule is the standard first-pass compute budget.

L4.prompt_tpl: For a linear layer with batch {B}, $d_{{\mathrm{{ in }}}}$ {di}, $d_{{\mathrm{{ out }}}}$ {do}, give forward, backward and total FLOPs. Answer with the total FLOPs.
L4.answer: Forward $2\cdot 32\cdot 768\cdot 3072 = 1.5100e8$; backward 2 * that = 3.0199e8; total 4.5299e8 FLOPs.
L4.explanation: Verified: $2\cdot 32\cdot 768\cdot 3072 = 150,994,944$; total 452,984,832. Exactly 6 FLOPs per parameter per sample: $6\cdot 768\cdot 3072\cdot 32 = 452,984,832$.

L4.prompt_tpl: A new layer needs {f}x fewer FLOPs than a dense layer but cannot be expressed as a gemm. Will it be faster in practice?
L4.answer: Usually not, or not by the FLOP ratio. Dense gemm runs near peak on tensor cores; an operation outside that path runs at a small fraction of peak and is typically memory-bound, so a 4-10x FLOP reduction routinely yields no speedup or a slowdown.
L4.explanation: The historical record here is consistent — unstructured sparsity, many depthwise and grouped convolution variants, and several efficient-attention schemes have shown exactly this gap. Measure wall clock; FLOPs are a proxy that this hardware breaks.

concepts.L2: Do not skip the problem sets. Watching 3Blue1Brown feels like learning and is not sufficient — it builds intuition that then needs to be made operational.

One amendment for this learner profile: Axler's Linear Algebra Done Right avoids determinants by design and de-emphasises computation, the wrong trade for someone who needs matrix computation as a working tool and the determinant-as-volume picture for Jacobians. Substitute Mathematics for Machine Learning (free PDF, ML-facing) and Strang 18.065 for depth, and fast.ai's Computational Linear Algebra for the numerical half 18.06 omits. L4.prompt_tpl: You have watched all of Essence of Linear Algebra and feel you understand {topic}. What is the next action?
L4.answer: Work problem sets — compute eigenvectors of specific matrices by hand, verify in numpy, and derive the results rather than recognising them. Intuition without operational fluency collapses at the first unfamiliar problem.
L4.explanation: The videos build the picture; the problem sets build the ability to use it. Skipping the second step is the single most common way this material fails to stick.

L4.prompt_tpl: For a career changer who needs matrix computation as a working tool, is Axler the right first book?
L4.answer: No.
L4.explanation: Linear Algebra Done Right avoids determinants by design and de-emphasises computation, which are precisely the things this learner needs early — determinants for Jacobians and change of variables, computation for everything numerical. L0.body:
$\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L$  iff  for every eps > 0 there is $\delta > 0$ with 0 < |x - a| < delta => |f(x) - L| < eps.
f continuous at a iff $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)$.
$\lim_{x\to 3} (x^{2} - 9)/(x - 3) = \lim (x+3) = 6$   (the hole is removable)
L0.cloze: A limit describes behaviour {{c1::near}} a point, not {{c2::at}} it; f is continuous at a iff {{c3::$\lim f(x) = f(a)$}}.

concepts.L1: A limit is the value a function approaches near a point, deliberately ignoring the value at the point. Continuity is the statement that the two agree. Every derivative in the subject is a limit, so this is the foundation, not a formality.
concepts.L2: The epsilon-delta definition is not there for rigour theatre — it is the template for every 'for any tolerance there exists a bound' argument in optimization and analysis, including convergence proofs for gradient descent. Learn to read it as a game: the adversary picks eps, you must produce delta.
concepts.L3: The definition quantifies 'close': for any target accuracy eps around L, you can force $f(x)$ within it by keeping x within some delta of a, excluding a itself. The exclusion $0 < |x - a|$ is what makes removable discontinuities work: $(x^{2}-9)/(x-3)$ is undefined at 3 but equals $x+3$ everywhere else, so the limit is 6. Continuity adds the requirement that $f(a)$ exists and equals that limit. Standard consequences used constantly: sums, products and compositions of continuous functions are continuous; a continuous function on a closed bounded set attains its maximum and minimum (Weierstrass), which is the existence theorem underneath 'a minimiser exists' in constrained optimization.

L4.prompt_tpl: Evaluate lim_{{x->{a}}} (x^2 - {a2})/(x - {a}).
L4.answer: 2a: for $a=3$ the limit is 6; for $a=5$ it is 10.
L4.explanation: Factor: $(x-a)(x+a)/(x-a) = x+a$ for $x \neq a$, so the limit is 2a. Verified numerically: $f(3.000001) = 6.000001$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does the definition of a limit exclude the point x = {a} itself?
L4.answer: So that a limit can exist where the function is undefined or has a different value. Derivatives require exactly this: the difference quotient is undefined at $h = 0$, yet its limit as $h \to 0$ is the derivative.
L4.explanation: Without the exclusion, no derivative could be defined at all — the whole of calculus depends on this one clause.

L4.prompt_tpl: $\mathrm{{ ReLU }}(x) = \max (0, x)$. Is it continuous at 0? Is it differentiable at 0?
L4.answer: Continuous yes; differentiable no.
L4.explanation: Left and right limits both give $0 = \mathrm{ReLU}(0)$, so it is continuous. The left derivative is 0 and the right is 1, so no derivative exists at 0. Frameworks return a subgradient (usually 0) there, which is a convention, not a derivative.

concepts.t: The derivative as best linear approximation

L0.body:
$f^{\prime}(a) = \lim_{h\to 0} (f(a+h) - f(a))/h$.
Equivalently: $f(a+h) = f(a) + f^{\prime}(a)h + o(h)$, i.e. the error is smaller than linear in h.
Tangent line: $L(x) = f(a) + f^{\prime}(a)(x - a)$.
$\sqrt{4.1} \approx 2 + (1/4)(0.1) = 2.025$  (true 2.02484568)
L0.cloze: $f(a+h) = f(a)$ + {{c1::$f^{\prime}(a)h$}} + $o(h)$; the derivative is the {{c2::slope of the best linear approximation}}, and the error is {{c3::$o(h)$}}.

concepts.L1: The derivative is the coefficient of the best linear approximation to f near a: the unique number making the remainder shrink faster than h. Reading it as 'slope of the tangent' is fine in one dimension; reading it as 'best linear model of f locally' is the version that generalises to Jacobians and to Taylor series.
concepts.L2: Taking the linearisation view rather than the slope view from the start is what makes multivariable calculus painless later: the Jacobian is then obviously the matrix of the best linear approximation, not a mysterious grid of partials. It is also what makes linearised analyses like NTK coherent.
concepts.L3: Rearranging the limit definition, $(f(a+h) - f(a))/h \to f^{\prime}(a)$ means $f(a+h) - f(a) - f^{\prime}(a)h = h \cdot \epsilon (h)$ with $\epsilon (h) \to 0$ — the remainder is $o(h)$. Uniqueness: if two constants m1 and m2 both worked, subtracting gives $(m_{1} - m_{2})h = o(h)$, forcing $m_{1} = m_{2}$. So 'differentiable' means 'admits a linear approximation with $o(h)$ error', and the derivative is that approximation's coefficient. Differentiability implies continuity (let $h \to 0$). The converse fails: $|x|$ at 0 is continuous, and its difference quotient tends to -1 from the left and +1 from the right, so no single linear approximation works.

L4.prompt_tpl: Use linearisation at a = {a} to estimate sqrt({x}), and give the error. Answer with the linearised estimate.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy: $\sqrt{4.1} = 2.0248456731316584$, so the linearisation overshoots by 0.000154. The error is $O(h^{2}) = O(0.01)$ times the second-derivative scale, consistent with what we see.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that differentiability at a implies continuity at a.
L4.answer: $f(a+h) - f(a) = f^{\prime}(a)h + o(h) \to 0$ as $h \to 0$, so $\lim f(a+h) = f(a)$.
L4.explanation: The converse fails: $|x|$ is continuous at 0 but has no derivative there, because the one-sided difference quotients disagree.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why 'derivative = best linear approximation' generalises to $\mathbb{{ R }}^{{ n }} \to \mathbb{{ R }}^{{ m }}$ but 'derivative = slope' does not.
L4.answer: In higher dimensions the local model is a linear map, not a number: $f(a+h) = f(a) + J h + o(\|h\|)$, where J is the Jacobian. 'Slope' has no meaning for a map between spaces of different dimension; 'best linear approximation' does.
L4.explanation: This is precisely the definition of the Frechet derivative, and taking it as primary makes the chain rule 'compose the linear approximations', which is one line instead of an index calculation.

concepts.t: Derivative rules and the chain rule in one variable

L0.body:
(fg)' = f'g + fg';  $(f/g)$' = (f'g - fg')/$g^{2}; (f(g(x)))$' = $f^{\prime}(g(x)) g^{\prime}(x)$.
$d/dx e^{x} = e^{x}; d/dx \ln x = 1/x; d/dx x^{n} = n x^{n-1}$.
$\sigma (x) = 1/(1+e^{-x}); \sigma$'$(x) = \sigma (x)(1 - \sigma (x))$.
tanh'$(x) = 1 - \tanh^{2}(x)$
L0.cloze: (f o g)'(x) = {{c1::$f^{\prime}(g(x)) g^{\prime}(x)$}};  sigma'(x) = {{c2::$\sigma (x)(1 - \sigma (x))$}};  d/dx ln x = {{c3::$1/x$}}.

concepts.L1: The chain rule says the derivative of a composition is the product of the derivatives evaluated at the right points. It is the single most important rule in machine learning, because a neural network is a composition and backpropagation is the chain rule applied systematically.
concepts.L2: sigma' = $\sigma (1 - \sigma)$ has maximum 0.25, so a stack of n sigmoid layers multiplies at most $0.25^{n}$ into the gradient — that is the vanishing gradient problem in one line, and it is why ReLU (derivative exactly 1 on the positive half) replaced it. Compute the number before believing the story.
concepts.L3: Chain rule via linearisation: near $a, g(a+h) = g(a) + g^{\prime}(a)h + o(h)$, and near $g(a), f(g(a)+k) = f(g(a)) + f^{\prime}(g(a))k + o(k)$. Substituting $k = g^{\prime}(a)h + o(h)$ gives $f(g(a+h)) = f(g(a)) + f^{\prime}(g(a))g^{\prime}(a)h + o(h)$, so the composite's best linear approximation has coefficient $f^{\prime}(g(a))g^{\prime}(a)$ — composing linear approximations multiplies their coefficients. Sigmoid: $\sigma = (1+e^{-x})^{-1}$, so sigma' = $e^{-x}/(1+e^{-x})^{2} = \sigma \cdot (e^{-x}/(1+e^{-x})) = \sigma (1-\sigma)$; its maximum is at $x = 0$ where $\sigma = 1/2$, giving 0.25.

L4.prompt_tpl: Differentiate f(x) = e^{{{a}x^2}} and evaluate at $x = 1$.
L4.explanation: Chain rule with outer $e^{u}$ and inner $u = 3x^{2}$, u' = 6x. Verified in numpy: $6\cdot \exp (3) = 120.5132215$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compute sigma'({x}) where sigma is the logistic function. Answer with the derivative of the logistic function at x.
L4.explanation: Verified in numpy. 0.25 is the global maximum of sigma', attained only at 0 — the best case for gradient flow through a sigmoid.

L4.prompt_tpl: A network stacks {n} sigmoid layers, each at its maximum derivative. What is the largest possible product of the activation derivatives?
L4.explanation: Verified: $0.25^{5} = 0.0009765625; 0.25^{10} = 9.5367e-07$. Even in the best case the gradient shrinks by a factor of a million over ten layers. ReLU's derivative of 1 removes this factor entirely.

L0.body:
$df/dx_{i} = \lim_{h\to 0} (f(x + h e_{i}) - f(x))/h$  — vary one coordinate, freeze the rest.
$f(x,y) = x^{2} y + y^{3}: df/dx = 2$xy,  $df/dy = x^{2} + 3y^{2}$.
Mixed partials commute for $C^{2}$ functions (Clairaut/Schwarz): $d^{2}f/dxdy = d^{2}f/dydx$.
L0.cloze: A partial derivative varies {{c1::one coordinate}} and freezes the others; for $C^{2}$ functions mixed partials {{c2::commute}}, which makes the Hessian {{c3::symmetric}}.

concepts.L1: A partial derivative is an ordinary derivative along one coordinate axis with all other coordinates held constant. Every technique from single-variable calculus applies verbatim; the only new thing is remembering what is being held fixed.
concepts.L2: Having all partial derivatives does not make a function differentiable. Partials probe only the axis directions, and a function can behave perfectly along both axes and be discontinuous elsewhere. Differentiability needs one linear map working in every direction — which is why the Jacobian is the real derivative.
concepts.L3: The classic counterexample: $f(x,y) = xy/(x^{2}+y^{2})$ with $f(0,0) = 0$ has both partials equal to 0 at the origin (f vanishes on both axes) but takes the value 1/2 along $y = x$, so it is not even continuous there, let alone differentiable. The sufficient condition is that the partials exist and are continuous near the point, in which case f is differentiable and the Jacobian is the matrix of partials. Clairaut's theorem: if the second partials are continuous then $d^{2}f/dxdy = d^{2}f/dydx$ — proved by applying the mean value theorem twice to the mixed second difference and letting both increments go to zero — which is why the Hessian is symmetric and why eigh applies to it.

L4.prompt_tpl: $f(x,y) = x^{{2}} y + y^{{3}}$. Compute both partials at ({x},{y}). Answer with df/dy.
L4.explanation: At $(2,1): 2\cdot 2\cdot 1 = 4$ and $4 + 3 = 7$. Verified in numpy by finite differences. Each partial holds the other variable fixed, which is why they only assemble into a gradient once a basis is fixed.

L4.prompt_tpl: For $f(x,y) = x^{{2}} y + y^{{3}}$, verify that the mixed partials commute.
L4.answer: $d/dy(2xy) = 2x$ and $d/dx(x^{2} + 3y^{2}) = 2x$. They agree.
L4.explanation: f is a polynomial, hence C^infinity, so Clairaut guarantees this. It is the reason the Hessian is symmetric and can be handled with eigh.

L4.prompt_tpl: A function has both partial derivatives at the origin but is not continuous there. How is that possible?
L4.answer: Partials only sample the two axis directions. $f(x,y) = xy/(x^{2}+y^{2}), f(0,0)=0$, is identically zero on both axes so both partials are 0, but equals 1/2 along $y = x$, so it has no limit at the origin.
L4.explanation: Differentiability is a statement about all directions simultaneously, captured by a single linear map. This is exactly why the Jacobian is the derivative and the list of partials is only its matrix when things are well behaved.

L4.prompt_tpl: $f(x,y) = x^{{2}} y + y^{{3}}$. Compute grad f at ({x},{y}) and the directional derivative along $u = [3,4]/5$. Answer with the directional derivative along u.
L4.explanation: Verified: $[4,7] \cdot [0.6,0.8] = 2.4 + 5.6 = 8.0$. Compare $\|\nabla f\| = \sqrt{65} = 8.0623$, the maximum over all unit directions — this u is nearly optimal.

L4.prompt_tpl: Feature 1 is measured in metres and feature 2 in millimetres. What does that do to the gradient direction and to gradient descent?
L4.answer: It rescales one gradient component by 1000, so the steepest-descent direction is dominated by the small-scale feature and the loss surface becomes highly elongated. Convergence slows in proportion to the resulting condition number.
L4.explanation: The gradient is not invariant under rescaling of inputs. This is the entire argument for standardising features, and the reason per-parameter adaptive methods partially compensate for it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that grad f is orthogonal to the level set of f through x.
L4.answer: Let $c(t)$ be a curve in the level set with $c(0) = x$. Then $f(c(t))$ is constant, so differentiating gives $\nabla f \cdot c^{\prime}(0) = 0$ for every tangent vector $c^{\prime}(0)$.
L4.explanation: This is what makes the Lagrange multiplier condition geometric: at a constrained optimum, the objective's gradient must be perpendicular to the constraint surface, i.e. parallel to the constraint's gradient.

For $f: \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, J_{ij} = df_{i}/dx_{j}$,  shape m x n.
$f(x + h) = f(x) + J h + o(\|h\|)$.
$m = 1: J$ is the gradient transposed (a row).  $n = m: |\det J|$ is the local volume scaling factor (change of variables).
torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(f, x)
L0.cloze: The Jacobian of $f: \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ has shape {{c1::m x n}}; it is the matrix of the {{c2::best linear approximation}}; |det J| gives the local {{c3::volume scaling}}.

concepts.L1: The Jacobian is the matrix of the best linear approximation to a vector-valued function: row i is the gradient of output i, column j says how all outputs respond to input j. Its determinant, when square, is the local volume scaling factor.
concepts.L2: Shape discipline is the practical skill. An m x n Jacobian for a 4096-wide layer is 16.7 million entries and is never materialised — frameworks compute Jacobian-vector or vector-Jacobian products instead. Any derivation that requires writing down a full Jacobian for a large layer has gone wrong.
concepts.L3: Differentiability at x means there is a linear map L with $f(x+h) = f(x) + Lh + o(\|h\|); L$ is unique, and taking $h = t e_{j}$ and letting $t \to 0$ shows its j-th column is $df/dx_{j}$, so L is the matrix of partials. When $n = m$, the change-of-variables formula for integrals carries the factor |det J| because the map takes an infinitesimal box to a parallelepiped whose volume is scaled by exactly the determinant of the local linear approximation — connecting this directly to determinant-as-volume, and it is why normalizing flows track log|det J|. In deep learning the Jacobian of a linear layer $y = Wx$ is simply W, which is the fact that makes backprop a matrix multiplication.

L4.prompt_tpl: $f(x,y) = (x^{{2}} y, x + \sin y)$. Compute the Jacobian at ({x},{y}) and its determinant. Answer with the determinant of the Jacobian.
L4.explanation: At $(1,0): 2\cdot 1\cdot 0 = 0, 1^{2} = 1, 1, \cos 0 = 1$. $\det ([[0,1],[1,1]]) = 0\cdot 1 - 1\cdot 1 = -1$. Verified in numpy. The negative sign means the map reverses orientation locally.

L4.prompt_tpl: A layer maps R^{n} -> R^{m}. What is the shape of its Jacobian and how many entries does it have? Answer with the number of entries.
L4.explanation: Verified: $4096^{2} = 16777216$; times 4 bytes = 67.1 MB for one layer. This is why reverse-mode AD computes $v^{T} J$ directly instead of forming J.

L4.prompt_tpl: For $y = Wx$, what is $dy/dx$, and why does that make backprop cheap?
L4.answer: The Jacobian is exactly W. Reverse-mode then needs only $v^{T} W$, one matrix-vector product, rather than forming or storing any new object.
L4.explanation: The Jacobian of a linear map is the map. Every backward pass of a linear layer is therefore a gemm with the transposed weight, which is why training costs about 3x the forward pass rather than n times it.

concepts.t: The chain rule as composition of Jacobians

L0.body:
For $h = f o g, J_{h}(x) = J_{f}(g(x)) J_{g}(x)$   — matrix product, right to left.
Scalar loss: $dL/dx = (dL/dy)^{T} J = a$ vector-Jacobian product (VJP).
For a deep net: $dL/dx = J_{1}^{T} J_{2}^{T} \dots J_{n}^{T} (dL/dy)$ — evaluated right to left, never as matrices.
L0.cloze: Jacobians of a composition {{c1::multiply}}; a scalar loss makes the product a chain of {{c2::vector-Jacobian products}}, evaluated {{c3::right to left}}.

concepts.L1: The multivariable chain rule is matrix multiplication of Jacobians in the order of composition. That single sentence contains backpropagation: a deep network is a composition, so its Jacobian is a long matrix product, and the gradient of a scalar loss is that product applied to a vector.
concepts.L2: The association order is everything. Multiplying the Jacobians as matrices then applying the vector costs $O(n^{3})$ per layer; starting from the loss end and carrying a vector costs $O(n^{2})$. Same mathematics, wildly different cost — that is the whole content of 'backprop is reverse-mode AD'.
concepts.L3: From the linearisation view: $g(x+h) = g(x) + J_{g} h + o(h)$, and $f(g(x) + k) = f(g(x)) + J_{f} k + o(k)$. Substituting $k = J_{g} h + o(h)$ gives $(f o g)(x+h) = (f o g)(x) + J_{f} J_{g} h + o(h)$, so the composite's Jacobian is the product — because composing linear maps is composing matrices. For a scalar loss $L, dL/dx = J_{1}^{T} \dots J_{n}^{T} v$ where $v = dL/dy$ is a single vector. Evaluating right to left keeps a vector at every stage: n matrix-vector products, $O(n^{2})$ each. Evaluating left to right forms n x n matrices: $O(n^{3})$ each. Matrix multiplication is associative, so both give the identical answer, and only one is affordable.

L4.prompt_tpl: Layers have Jacobians of shape {s1}, {s2}, {s3} (in composition order g then h then f). What is the shape of the composite Jacobian, and in which order do the matrices multiply?
L4.explanation: The last layer's Jacobian is leftmost. Only this order type-checks, which is a useful shape-based memory aid for the composition order.

L4.prompt_tpl: Jacobians are all {n}x{n} and there are {L} layers. Compare the FLOP cost of left-to-right matrix products versus right-to-left vector products for a scalar loss. Answer with the FLOP cost of the right-to-left VJP chain.
L4.answer: Matrix chain: 9 matmuls at $2n^{3} = 2e9$ each = 1.8e10 FLOPs. VJP chain: 10 matvecs at $2n^{2} = 2e6$ each = 2e7 FLOPs. Ratio 900x.
L4.explanation: Verified: $9\cdot 2\cdot 1000^{3} = 1.8e10; 10\cdot 2\cdot 1000^{2} = 2e7$; ratio 900. In general the ratio is about $n \cdot (L-1)/L$, so it grows linearly with layer width.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the chain rule for Jacobians from the best-linear-approximation definition.
L4.answer: Substitute g's linearisation into f's: $f(g(x+h)) = f(g(x) + J_{g} h + o(h)) = f(g(x)) + J_{f}(J_{g} h) + o(h)$, so the composite's linear part is $J_{f} J_{g}$.
L4.explanation: No indices required. The index form $dh_{i}/dx_{k} = \sum_{j} (df_{i}/dg_{j})(dg_{j}/dx_{k})$ is just this matrix product written out entrywise.
